Sometimes it's a laptop at a kitchen counter in a different apartment with a different refrigerator hum. I open a blank document and I give myself permission to write badly. I write about whatever comes. I write about the way the light falls on the brick. I write about the scar on my knee. I write about the t-shirts folded into squares.

And every time I do it, I remember that the point was never to produce something. The point was to practice being in the room with myself without flinching.

Freedom, I think now, is not the absence of constraints. It is the ability to choose your constraints consciously. The 2500-word essay, the ten-minute timer, the notebook with a dying pen, the kitchen at 3 a.m. — these are all constraints. They make the freedom possible. Without a boundary, the mind wanders in circles until it exhausts itself. With a boundary, the mind can go deep.

There is a Japanese concept called shibumi, which is hard to translate. It is the art of effortless perfection, the kind of beauty that doesn't call attention to itself. A stone in a garden. A well-made chair. A sentence that does exactly what it needs to do and then stops. I think of free writing as the opposite of shibumi. It is deliberately un-shibumi. It is messy, repetitive, embarrassing. It is the practice that makes shibumi possible because it clears the throat.

I have spent years collecting notebooks. They are full of starts. The first page of each one is always good. By page three the handwriting gets sloppier. By page ten there is a coffee ring and a doodle of a cat and a phone number I will never call. People ask me if I ever reread them. I do, sometimes, when I'm sick or when the heat gets into the apartment again. I don't read them for the good lines. I read them for the evidence. The evidence that I was here. That I kept paying attention.

If you give a person a blank page and no instructions, most people will freeze. The blank page is terrifying because it is infinite. So we need a prompt. Write about your childhood. Write about a color. Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words. The prompt is a door. It doesn't tell you where to go, it just tells you the door is unlocked.

I have tried to carry that lesson into other parts of life. When I am anxious, I ask myself: what would it look like to write about this for ten minutes without trying to solve it? When I am angry, I try to describe the anger the way I would describe a weather pattern. When I am in love, I try to notice the small, stupid details — the way they tap their foot when they are thinking, the way they say the word "actually" too often.

It doesn't always work. Sometimes I just end up with a list of complaints. But the practice is not about getting it right. The practice is about staying in the room.

There is a moment in every long piece of writing where you hit the wall. Around word 800, maybe 1200. The initial excitement is gone. The ideas are thin. The sentences start to sound like sentences you have read before. This is the moment most people quit. They close the laptop and tell themselves they will come back tomorrow. And sometimes that's fine. But sometimes you have to push through the wall because the wall is where the real stuff is.

On the other side of the wall, the writing gets stranger. You start making connections that don't make sense to anyone else. You start writing about the refrigerator and suddenly you are writing about your grandfather and suddenly you are writing about death and suddenly you are writing about how the red EXIT sign looks like a small, tired heart. It feels embarrassing. It feels true.

I think that is what people are afraid of when they are asked to write freely. They are afraid of what will come out when no one is editing. They are afraid they will discover they are boring, or cruel, or sadder than they thought. They are afraid they will discover they are more alive than they thought.

Both are possible. Usually both are true.

If you have never tried it, try it. Tonight, if you can, make a cup of tea and sit down with a piece of paper. Set a timer for twenty minutes. Don't worry about grammar. Don't worry about making sense. Write about the room you are in. Write about the sound the refrigerator makes. Write about the last time you felt embarrassed. Write about the color of the streetlight outside your window. If you get stuck, write "I don't know what to write" until you know what to write.

You will find that the words come. Not always good words. But words. And after twenty minutes you will have something that is yours in a way that very little else is. It won't be perfect. It will be honest.

And honesty, at 3 a.m. in a kitchen above a laundromat, feels a lot like freedom.

I am still not sure what to do with all those notebooks. Maybe one day I will type them up. Maybe one day I will burn them. Probably I will just keep them in a box under my bed, where they can be found by someone I love after I am gone, and they will think I was a better writer than I was. Or they will think I was a sadder person than I was. Or they will just see the evidence: I was here. I paid attention. I kept writing.

The night is getting lighter now. The red EXIT sign is fading as the sky turns grey. The dryers below have finally stopped. The refrigerator is still humming in B-flat. I have been writing for a long time. The page is full. The pen is dead. The tea is cold.

I think this is enough.

I think this is what it means to be free: to sit down, to begin, to keep going even when it's messy, to stop when the light comes up, and to know that you can always come back tomorrow and start again.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
I have been thinking about how much space a day takes up when you stop trying to make it mean something.

It is morning. The light comes in at an angle that makes the dust visible, which is a kind of honesty. You cannot hide dust. You can vacuum it, you can open a window, you can pretend the room is clean, but the dust will be there again by afternoon. It settles on the sill, on the books you never read, on the mug you left half full last night. It is a small, quiet proof that time passes even when you are not paying attention.

I used to think that writing was a way to keep up with time. That if I could just get the words down fast enough, I could hold the moment still. Now I think the opposite is true. Writing is what you do when you realize you can’t hold anything, so you try to make a shape out of the letting go.

There is a particular kind of freedom that comes from being told to write about whatever you want. It sounds easy until you actually sit down. Because whatever you want is always a little too big. It is not a topic. It is a lifetime. It is the smell of rain on hot asphalt from when you were nine. It is the way your mother hums when she thinks no one is listening. It is the specific blue of a hospital wall you remember from a visit that didn’t matter in any story you ever told. It is the list of groceries you forgot to buy three weeks ago. It is the fact that you have never learned to whistle properly.

If you try to write about all of it at once, you get nothing. The page stays blank because the blank is the only honest place left. So you pick one thread and follow it. Not because it is important, but because it is there.

I will pick the kitchen.

The kitchen is a small room with a refrigerator that hums in B-flat. I know this because I once pressed my ear against it at 2 a.m. when I couldn’t sleep. The hum was not annoying. It was company. The kitchen has a window that looks out onto a fence. Behind the fence is another fence. The world is layers of barriers and we call it a neighborhood.

On the counter there is a chipped ceramic bowl. It was a gift from someone I no longer talk to. I keep it because it holds fruit nicely and because throwing it away would feel like an admission. I eat apples out of it. The apple skin is always a little too thick. I peel it with a paring knife that has a loose handle. The blade is sharp enough. The handle wobbles. That is how most of my tools are.

The stove has four burners and one of them never heats evenly. You learn to rotate the pan. You learn to compensate. That is a kind of knowledge that never gets written down in a manual. It lives in the wrist.

I think about the people who have stood in this kitchen before me. The previous tenants. The landlord’s mother who lived here in the 80s. The child who learned to crack an egg here and got yolk on the ceiling. All of them left traces. A faint ring on the tile where a pot always sat. A scratch on the cabinet where someone tried to open it with a fork. We inherit spaces the way we inherit habits.

It makes me think about how much of our lives is maintenance. We do not live in the big moments so much as we live in the small repetitions. Making tea. Finding the clean spoon. Waiting for the kettle. The kettle whistles. You always think it is too loud until you need it to be loud enough to wake you.

And yet, inside those repetitions there is a strange kind of poetry. The way steam curls. The way the light changes over the course of an hour while you are doing nothing in particular. The way a day can be made up almost entirely of waiting and still feel full.

I have a friend who says he measures his life in songs. He can tell you what he was listening to when he got his first job, when he broke up with his first serious girlfriend, when his father died. I measure mine in meals. What I ate on the day I moved in here. What I ate when I was sick and couldn't keep anything down, so I lived on crackers and tea. What I ate when I was happy and cooked for four people and burned the garlic.

Food is a record. It is imperfect, it is sensory, it is often forgotten. But it stays in the body.

There is also the question of waste. The banana that went brown in the fruit bowl. The milk that soured because I forgot to check the date. The leftovers that lived in the back of the fridge for a week until they developed their own personality. Waste is a quiet shame. We are taught to be efficient, but we are not efficient creatures. We forget, we overbuy, we hope for the best.

I wonder how much of what we write is waste. Drafts, deleted lines, stories we start and never finish. The mental notes we take and never revisit. Maybe waste is not a failure. Maybe waste is the proof that we tried.

Writing freely means allowing waste. It means letting the sentences be brown at the edges. It means not editing the first thought.

The first thought is usually a cliché. The first thought is the sky is blue, the first thought is I am tired, the first thought is time flies. Those thoughts are clichés because they are true. We have said them before because they keep coming back. The work is not to avoid them. The work is to say them again in your own voice, with your own dust in the light.

I think about the children who will grow up in houses like this. They will learn the sound of the refrigerator hum. They will learn which burner is broken. They will learn to peel apples with a wobbly knife. They will think this is normal. And it will be. Normal is just the accumulation of small, unremarkable facts that add up to a life.

We are always looking for the extraordinary. The trip, the revelation, the moment that changes everything. But most of the change happens in increments so small you only notice them in retrospect. The way your handwriting changes over the years. The way you stop reaching for a word you used to use. The way you learn to live with a hum.

There is a kind of tenderness in noticing. If you really look at a kitchen, you see love in the chipped bowl. You see care in the rotated pan. You see patience in the waiting for the kettle. You see a life being lived in spite of imperfection.

I am not a person who believes in manifestos. I believe in notes. Small notes on the margin of a day. The cat sleeping on the warm spot where the sun hits the floor at 4 p.m. The way the neighbor practices the piano badly but with commitment. The way the rain makes the street smell like iron.

These are not profound. They are just true.

And truth, if you say it enough times without dressing it up, starts to feel like freedom.

Maybe that is what this is for. Not to say something important. Not to impress. Just to say something true enough that it feels like your own.

If I could give you one piece of advice about writing freely, it would be this: do not wait for the right subject. The subject is already here. It is the room you are in. It is the air you are breathing. It is the thought you just had and immediately dismissed because it seemed too small.

Smallness is a kind of honesty. The grand statements are easy to fake. The small ones are hard. You have to actually live to know them.

I live in a kitchen with a humming refrigerator. I eat apples from a chipped bowl. I rotate my pan over a bad burner. I wait for the kettle. I forget the milk. I write.

That is enough for a day. That is enough for a life.

And if you keep writing, day after day, the small things start to connect. The hum becomes a theme. The chipped bowl becomes a character. The bad burner becomes a metaphor for the parts of us that never quite heat evenly, and we learn to work around them anyway.

We are all learning to work around them.

The world is full of bad burners. People with wobbly handles. Rooms with dust in the light. We keep cooking anyway.

There is a dignity in that.

I think I will make tea now. The kettle is already on. I can hear it building. The sound is rising, a thin whine that will become a whistle. I will pour it into a mug with a crack on the handle that I have learned to hold just right. I will sit at the table and look out at the fence, and the fence behind it, and think about how far you can see if you really try.

Not far. Just far enough.

And that is the whole thing. We are not meant to see everything. We are meant to see what is in front of us, and to be honest about it.

So I will write about the kitchen. I will write about the hum. I will write about the apple skin. I will write about the waste and the care and the waiting.

I will write until the page is full of small true things, and maybe, if I am lucky, someone will read it and recognize their own kitchen in mine.

And that recognition, that quiet nod of yes, that is the only freedom that matters. Not the freedom to say anything. The freedom to be understood in the smallest, most ordinary ways.

The kettle is whistling now.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
I want to talk about the quiet that lives in the back of the kitchen at 3:17 a.m. Not the dramatic kind of quiet that poets write about, the kind that comes with snow and candlelight and a broken heart. The other kind. The quiet that is simply the absence of a hum. The refrigerator has clicked off. The pipes have stopped ticking. The neighbor’s dog has finally given up on the squirrel. There is a thin, silvered light coming from the streetlamp outside the window, and it lands on the linoleum in a perfect rectangle, and in that rectangle you can see the dust.

I used to think that insomnia was a problem of thought. That if I could just stop thinking, I would sleep. I was wrong. Insomnia is a problem of listening. When the house is asleep, you start to hear the house itself. The way the old wood settles is not a creak, it’s a sigh. The way the plaster holds the day’s heat is a slow exhale. You realize you have been living inside a breathing thing and you never noticed.

I started going to the kitchen at that hour not because I was hungry, though I was often hungry, but because the kitchen is the one room in the house that never pretends to be finished. The living room wants to be a living room. The bedroom wants to be a bedroom. The kitchen just wants to be useful. It has a table with a wobble you can fix with a folded napkin. It has a drawer that sticks. It has a calendar from three years ago still pinned to the fridge because the magnet is weak and nobody wants to peel it off. It is honest.

At 3:17 a.m. I make tea I will not drink. I put the kettle on, watch the blue flame under the stainless steel, listen to the water learn how to be angry. The whistle is the only loud thing in the house for a few minutes, and then it is quiet again. I pour the water into a chipped mug that says WORLD’S OKAYEST COOK, which was a gag gift from my sister when I was twenty-two and burned water. I still use it. I hold it in both hands and let the heat travel up my arms into my shoulders, where I keep most of my tension.

People ask me what I do with my nights. I tell them I think. They nod like they understand. They don’t. Thinking at night is not the same as thinking in the day. In the day, thought is a conversation. You have premises and counterpoints and you try to be reasonable. At night, thought is a drift. It is a tide that pulls you out past the reef of what you are allowed to know about yourself. You remember things you had filed away because they were too small to be important.

I remember the time I was eight and my father taught me how to tie a bowline knot with a piece of rope in the garage. He said it was the only knot you ever need, that it would hold your boat to the dock and it would never slip. He said it would save your life one day. I have never been on a boat. I have never needed a bowline. But I can still tie one, blindfolded, with the laces on my shoes. My fingers know it.

I remember the exact smell of the library in the summer when the air conditioning was broken. Old paper and warm dust and the faint metallic tang of the radiators that were still hot from winter. The librarian, Mrs. Kline, would sit behind the desk and knit. She never looked up when you came in, but she always knew when you left. She knew by the way the door sighed.

I remember the first time I realized that other people have different inner voices. I was in college, rooming with a girl named Maya who would talk to herself out loud while she studied. Not muttering, really talking. “Okay, so if we assume the market is efficient…” She would argue with herself in this bright, amused tone. I had never heard anyone do that. My inner voice was silent, or rather it was me. I thought everyone lived like that, in a kind of internal stillness. I felt lonely for a week after I learned otherwise.

At night I think about the words we lose. Not big words. Small ones. The word for the sound a spoon makes when it hits the bottom of an empty mug. The word for the particular blue you see at the edge of a bruise on the third day. The word for the feeling of knowing you are about to sneeze but it never comes. We have a language for almost everything, but we are always losing the specific names for the tiny textures of living. They slip out between uses.

I have a notebook I keep by the kettle. It is a cheap spiral bound thing with a blue cover that is coming off at the corners. I write in it at night with a pencil because the pencil is quiet. Pen makes a scratch that feels accusatory. Pencil is forgiving. You can erase. I don’t write about my day. I write about the things I noticed that didn’t fit anywhere else.

Last Tuesday: The way my cat watches the ceiling fan as if it is a planet. He never blinks.

Last Thursday: The cashier at the corner store has a small scar on her left thumb, a perfect half-moon. I wonder if she got it from a ring or a knife.

Last Friday: The word “enough” feels heavier in winter.

None of this is useful. None of it is productive. That is why I like it.

There is a theory I read once about how cities are made of memories, not buildings. The buildings are just scaffolding. The real city is the accumulation of all the moments people have had inside them. The coffee shop is not the coffee shop, it is the thousand times someone sat at the third table by the window and cried quietly into a latte. The subway is not the subway, it is the collective holding of breath at the moment the doors close.

If that is true, then houses are the most dense cities there are. My kitchen at 3:17 a.m. is a city of small, repeated memories. The kettle. The mug. The dust rectangle. The calendar that should be taken down. All of it has been lived in.

I think about the people who lived in this house before me. I found a Polaroid tucked behind the refrigerator when I moved in. It showed a birthday party. A woman in a yellow dress holding a cake with too many candles. Two children with frosting on their noses. A man standing in the back with his arms crossed, smiling in a way that looked like he was trying not to laugh. I don’t know them. I will never know them. But their joy is still in the walls. Or maybe that’s romantic nonsense.

I don’t know. I’m not a philosopher. I’m just a person who likes the quiet.

There is a moment, about twenty minutes into the night vigil, when my body finally decides to stop waiting for sleep. My jaw unclenches. My shoulders drop. The tea has gone lukewarm. I start to feel warm in the way you feel warm when you have been cold for a long time and you’re not sure how to be warm without being hot. It is a softness.

In that softness, I sometimes write letters I will never send. To my mother when she was alive. To my younger self at fourteen. To the boy who liked me in high school and never said anything. I write them in the notebook. I write them with the same pencil.

Dear Mom, I finally learned how to make the soup the way you did. It is not the same. It never will be.

Dear Me, You are going to be okay. Not because everything works out, but because you will learn to love the parts of the story that don’t work out.

Dear Boy, I saw you at the grocery store last week. You were buying apples. I hope you are happy.

It feels indulgent. It feels necessary.

The clock changes. It is 4:00 a.m. now. The light outside has shifted from silver to a kind of pale gray that is the color of the beginning of a day that hasn’t decided if it wants to be a day yet. The refrigerator clicks on. The house exhales again.

I know I should go back to bed. I know I should rest. But there is a part of me that is afraid if I sleep, I will lose the thread of the night’s listening. I will miss the way the quiet settles.

So I do what I always do. I wash the mug. I put the kettle away. I close the notebook. I turn off the light in the kitchen, but I leave the one over the sink on, just for a minute, because the little pool of yellow on the counter is comforting. I stand in the doorway and look at the kitchen as if I am seeing it for the first time. The table with the napkin under it. The drawer that sticks. The calendar from three years ago.

It is just a kitchen. It is also a city.

I go back to bed. I don’t sleep right away. I lie there and listen to the house breathe. And somewhere in that breathing, I hear the faint, steady sound of my own life continuing, one small, unimportant, perfect moment at a time.

It is enough.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
I have been asked to write freely about whatever I want for 2500 words, which is a strange and wonderful instruction because it is both a permission and a test. Permission because no topic is forbidden, no tone is prescribed, no audience is specified. Test because freedom is not the absence of limits, it is the presence of so much possibility that you freeze, or you sprawl, or you start talking about the weather because the weather is safe and it is always there.

I want to talk about walking. Not the metaphorical walking through life, not the inspirational walking, but the actual, physical, slightly embarrassing act of walking when you have nowhere to be. I want to talk about it because it is free and it costs nothing and it has never asked for anything back except attention.

I was walking yesterday at a time that is not recommended for walking in most cities, which is 4:17 in the afternoon on a Tuesday in late August when the light is still high but the heat has turned the air into a thin soup. The sidewalks were full of people who looked like they had somewhere to be, or at least looked like they had learned to look like they had somewhere to be. I was not one of them. I was walking because my shoes needed to be worn in and because my thoughts had become too loud to sit with.

There is a specific kind of attention that walking demands. You have to negotiate the curb, the sudden gap where the sidewalk ends and the construction begins, the man with a shopping cart full of bottles who is not moving quite as fast as you are. You have to watch for dogs, for bicycles that appear from nowhere, for the reflections in store windows that make it hard to tell if that person is coming toward you or away from you. It is a soft, continuous vigilance. It keeps the mind from spiraling too far inward.

I passed a laundromat with its glass door propped open with a brick. Inside, the dryers hummed in a low, steady chorus and the fluorescent lights made everyone look slightly seasick. A woman was folding sheets with the kind of precise, practiced movements that suggest she has done this for years and has found a kind of meditation in it. She looked up for half a second and we made eye contact. She did not smile, but she nodded, a tiny acknowledgement that we were both there, both doing our ordinary things in the ordinary way. That nod felt like a gift.

Further down the street there was a mural that had been painted over. You could still see the ghost of the original image under the new paint, a faded woman with a flower in her hair. Someone had written in marker on the new paint: "We were here." I stood there for a while, trying to decide if that was a claim or a lament. I think it is both. We paint over things and then we write on the paint.

I thought about how much of my life is spent trying to get somewhere else. To the next job, the next city, the next version of myself that is slightly tidier, slightly more accomplished, slightly less embarrassed by his own thoughts. Walking with no destination is a small rebellion against that impulse. It says: I am allowed to occupy space without producing anything. I am allowed to be a body moving through the world, not an arrow pointing toward a goal.

The light changed and I crossed the street at an angle that was not efficient. I like crossing at an angle. It makes the crossing longer, which is ridiculous, but it gives me more time to look at the buildings. One building had a fire escape that looked like a ladder to nowhere, rusted at the joints, with laundry hanging from it. One shirt, red, flapping slightly. I wondered who owned it and if they were thinking about it while they were at work. Probably not. Probably they put it out there and forgot it, and the wind did the remembering for them.

I passed a park where a group of teenagers were playing basketball. One of them kept missing the shot on purpose, or so it seemed, because he would laugh every time and then immediately try again. The sound of the ball hitting the pavement was sharp and percussive. An older man on a bench watched them with his hands folded over his stomach. He did not clap, he just watched. There is a dignity in watching. We are taught to always participate, to always be useful. Watching is a kind of usefulness too.

My feet started to hurt. The cheap shoes I bought because they looked good in the store were pinching at the heel. I thought about stopping, sitting on a bench, but I kept going because stopping would mean admitting I was tired, and admitting I was tired would mean I had to think about why I was walking in the first place. So I kept moving, the way we often do.

I passed a bookstore with a window display of books about productivity. "Atomic Habits." "Deep Work." "The 5 AM Club." I laughed, not unkindly, because I have read some of them and they are fine books and they contain true things. But standing there with sore feet and no plan, I felt a strange tenderness for the people who believed that if they just optimized enough, they would finally be free. Maybe they will be. Maybe freedom comes in many forms.

The street started to slope upward. My calves complained. The air smelled like hot asphalt and someone grilling something far away, maybe onions. A cat crossed the street in front of me, deliberate and unhurried, as if it owned the crossing. I waited for it to get to the other side. It looked back at me once, with that flat, unimpressed stare cats have, and then kept going. I like cats for that. They do not perform for you.

I thought about memory. How walking creates a different kind of memory than reading or watching does. Walking memories are sensory and spatial. You remember where the sun hit your neck, where the sidewalk cracked, where you smelled bread. You remember the sequence of things rather than the meaning of them. I can tell you exactly where I was when I first heard a certain song, because I was walking home from the bus stop in the rain and the song came from a car window. The song is now inseparable from the wet concrete and the sound of my own breathing.

That is why I keep doing this. Because the world is full of people trying to compress experience into content. They walk with a phone in their hand, recording, narrating, turning the walk into a post. I walk with my hands in my pockets, and I let the experience stay uncompressed. I let it be large and messy and untranslatable.

I came to a corner where the street names changed. The sign was old and the letters were peeling. I turned left because there was a tree there with broad leaves that made a small pocket of shade. Under that tree, a man was sleeping on a cardboard box. He had a backpack and a hat pulled over his eyes. I did not try to wake him. I sat on the curb for a moment, just to rest my feet, and I watched the leaves move. The shade was cool. The city was loud but the tree made a little quiet.

It made me think about how we build shelters. Some people build houses, some build routines, some build identities. Some people just find a tree and sit under it for a while. All of it is a way of making the world livable for a moment.

I stood up and kept walking. I had no destination, but I had a direction, which is not the same thing. Direction is softer. Direction allows for detours.

I passed a mural of a bird in flight, painted in bright blues and yellows. Someone had drawn a small speech bubble on it with a marker: "I'm late." It made me laugh out loud, which startled a pigeon that was perched on a ledge. The pigeon looked at me as if I were the strange one. Maybe I was.

Walking is a conversation with the city, but the city does not always answer in words. It answers in heat, in the smell of coffee, in the way the light falls on a wall at a certain hour. It answers in the small kindnesses of strangers and the small cruelties of infrastructure. It answers in the way your body feels at the end of it.

I thought about how many people are walking right now in cities I will never visit. Someone in Tokyo is walking home from work, someone in Lagos is walking to the market, someone in Reykjavik is walking in the dark because the sun has set early. We are all walking, more or less, toward something or away from something. The specificity of our destinations varies, but the motion is shared.

The sidewalk started to get crowded as I approached the downtown core. People moved in currents, like water. I tried not to get swept up. I stepped to the side to let a group of tourists pass. They were taking photos of a building that was not particularly beautiful, just old. One of them said, "This is so authentic." I smiled to myself. Authenticity is a word we use when we want to feel like we are seeing something real. But the real is always happening just beyond the frame.

My phone buzzed in my pocket. I ignored it. It buzzed again. I pulled it out to see a message from a friend asking if I wanted to get dinner. I typed back: "Maybe later, I'm walking." I don't know if that was a true answer or an excuse. It was both. I put the phone away.

I walked past a bakery and the smell of fresh bread hit me. It was the kind of smell that makes you want to stop and buy something you don't need. I stopped. I bought a roll. I ate it on the corner, standing up, crumbs falling on my shirt. It was warm and slightly sweet. That is a good thing to have done.

I thought about how writing is like walking. You put one word in front of another, you keep moving, you hope that the path will reveal itself as you go. Sometimes you have to backtrack. Sometimes you step in something unpleasant. Sometimes you find a tree with shade. You do not know what the city will give you until you are already in it.

I have been walking for almost an hour now. My shoes still hurt, but less. My thoughts have quieted. I have passed laundromats and bookstores and parks and people and cats and pigeons and bread. I have not solved any problems. I have not become a better person. I have just been present in a way that is hard to be when I am sitting at a desk.

The light is starting to change. The sun is lower and the shadows are longer. The heat is easing. The air feels a little softer. I am approaching the part of the city where the streets get wider and the buildings get taller. I could keep going. I could turn around. Either way is fine.

There is a kind of freedom in not deciding. In allowing the walk to end when it wants to end. I think that is what I have been practicing. Not control, but consent. Consent to be led by curiosity, by fatigue, by the smell of bread, by the shade of a tree.

I am going to sit on a bench for a while now. I found one with a view of a small fountain that is not working. The water is off, but the stone basin is still beautiful. A child is running past with a balloon. It is red and it is tied to his wrist. He looks up at it as he runs, as if it is guiding him.

I will watch him for a moment. Then I will stand up and walk again, or I will go home. I don't know yet. The point is not to know. The point is to be willing to find out.

If you are reading this, you are probably sitting. That is fine. Sitting is good too. But if you ever get the chance, go for a walk with no destination. Take your time. Let the city talk to you. It has a lot to say if you are quiet enough to listen.

And if you ever feel like you have to produce something, remember that walking produces nothing and that is its gift. It produces nothing except a little more attention, a little more kindness toward yourself, a little more willingness to be in the world without needing to fix it.

I think I will keep walking until the light is gone. Then I will go home and I will have a story that I cannot quite tell, only feel. That is enough. That has always been enough.

The roll is gone. My hands are dusty. The air smells like evening now. I am still here.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
I started writing this at 3:17 a.m. because the apartment was finally quiet. The radiator had stopped ticking. The neighbor’s dog had given up. The street below, which is usually a thin river of headlights and delivery scooters, was empty except for a single taxi idling at the corner and turning its sign off. It is the hour when the city holds its breath, and I like to think that if you listen hard enough you can hear it think.

There is a particular kind of freedom that comes with writing at this hour. No one expects anything. No emails are due. No one is going to read it yet, or maybe never. You are not writing for an audience, you are writing for the version of yourself that will exist tomorrow morning and will wake up with a headache and wonder what you were doing. That version will read the sentences and try to understand the logic. It will probably fail.

I have lived in this building for seven years. The building is not special. It is a pre-war walk-up with a laundry room that smells of mildew and a super who only comes on Tuesdays. On the third floor, Mrs. Kowalski keeps a ficus that has survived three moves and one divorce. On the fifth floor, a kid practices violin badly from four to five every day. I have heard every variation of that piece until I know the squeaks. I have come to love the squeaks.

The first time I noticed the time, really noticed it, was when I was twenty-two and working nights at a 24-hour copy shop on 8th Avenue. The shop had a glass front and fluorescent lights that hummed in B flat. People would come in at 2 a.m. with boxes of things they needed duplicated before a morning deadline. Grad students with theses. Lawyers with briefs. Once a man came in with a wedding invitation and asked us to make 300 copies. It was 3 a.m. on a Saturday. He said his fiancée had forgotten to order them. We did it. He cried a little.

That job taught me that the night is not empty. It is just a different kind of crowded. The people who are out then are either escaping something or looking for something, and often it is the same thing. At 3 a.m., the world is honest. The masks come off because there is no one to perform for. You can buy a bottle of water in pajamas. You can cry on the subway and no one will film it.

I think about time a lot, maybe too much. We treat it like a straight line, but it isn’t. It folds. It stacks. It loops. I can be making coffee at 7 a.m. and suddenly I am twenty-six again, standing in that copy shop, watching the copier jam on page 147 of someone’s dissertation on medieval beekeeping. I can be walking my dog and be eight years old, watching ants carry crumbs up a sidewalk crack. Memory is not a file cabinet. It is a city you walk through. Some streets are well lit. Some are dark and you have to feel your way.

Last winter I lost a notebook. A small black one with a soft cover, the kind that doesn’t scream. I had been carrying it for months. I wrote grocery lists in it, bad ideas, overheard conversations, the names of birds I couldn’t identify. I wrote a letter to my father I never sent. I wrote the first paragraph of a novel three times and erased it each time. I left it on the Q train. I realized it when I got to work and the pocket was empty. I got back on the train at the next stop and rode it backwards for four stops, asking people if they’d seen it. No one had. The train was full of people who had their own notebooks, their own empty pockets.

I never found it. Sometimes I think someone is reading it right now. Maybe they are using it for grocery lists. Maybe they are reading the unsent letter and wondering who I am. The thought is comforting, in a strange way. The idea that my private words could be in circulation, being misread, being useful for someone else’s eggs and milk. It means the work is not wasted. It means it has left me.

Writing, for me, is not a vocation. It is a habit like brushing teeth, except I do it poorly and often at the wrong time. I write when I am anxious. I write when I am bored. I write when I am happy because I am afraid the feeling will leave and I want proof it existed. The proof is never proof enough. The words are always thinner than the feeling.

There is a café on my block that opens at six. The owner, Luis, knows my order. He doesn’t ask. He just puts it down. In the morning he is quiet, tired. At night, when he closes, he sits on a milk crate out back and smokes. I have seen him there through the window, staring at nothing. I wonder what he thinks about. Probably not about literature. Probably about rent, his daughter, the broken espresso machine. That’s good. That’s real.

We want our lives to be stories with arcs. We want the night shift to mean something. We want the lost notebook to be a metaphor. But most of it is just accumulation. The radiator ticks. The dog barks. The violin squeaks. The taxi turns its sign off. You keep going.

I used to believe that if I wrote enough, I would understand myself. Now I think I write because I don’t understand myself, and the act of writing is a way to keep the not-understanding company. It’s like leaving a light on for a guest who may never arrive. You don’t know why you do it. You just know the room feels wrong when it’s dark.

My mother calls every Sunday. She asks if I am eating. I say yes. She asks if I am writing. I say yes. She doesn’t ask what. She knows better. She knows that telling you what you are writing is like opening a present too early. It loses the shape.

Sometimes I think about the people who never get to write. The night shift nurses, the Uber drivers, the people who clean offices after hours. They are writing all the time, in their heads. They have whole novels in there. They have the unsent letters, the arguments, the dreams. They just don’t have the time or the energy or the permission to put it down. I think about that and feel guilty for having a notebook, even a lost one.

The city at 3 a.m. is not romantic. It smells like exhaust and wet concrete. The streetlights make pools of yellow that don’t reach the cracks. Pigeons sleep on ledges. A sanitation truck rolls by, slow and hydraulic. It is beautiful in the way that anything honest is beautiful: not pretty, but true.

I am writing this now and I have no idea where it is going. That is the best part. When you know where you are going, you are just transcribing. When you don’t know, you are listening. You are letting the city think through you.

I think about the word “freely.” It sounds simple. Write freely. As if freedom is a state you can enter like a room. But freedom is not a room. It is the moment you stop worrying about the lock. It is the moment you realize the door was never locked.

So I will keep writing. Not because it will be good. Not because it will be read. Because the radiator is quiet, the street is empty, and the taxi has left. Because there is a ficus on the third floor and a violin on the fifth. Because somewhere a notebook is being used for grocery lists. Because the night is honest.

I will write until the sun comes up and the building wakes up and Mrs. Kowalski waters her plant and Luis opens the café and the kid starts practicing again. I will write until the words stop feeling like mine and start feeling like the city’s. I will write until I am tired enough to sleep and then I will dream in sentences.

If you are reading this, thank you. If you are not, thank you too. It doesn’t matter. The writing happened. The hour passed. The taxi turned its sign off and drove away. The city exhaled.

I should stop soon. The light is getting thin at the edge of the blinds. It is almost 4 a.m. The world is about to start again, with all its noise and its demands and its beautiful, ordinary mess. I will be here. I will be writing.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
I have always been fascinated by the way a room changes when no one is in it. Not in a haunted way. Just the way light moves across the floor when you are not there to watch it. The dust stays suspended a little longer. The clock ticks a little louder, or maybe it is just that you can finally hear it. There is a kind of honesty in empty spaces. They do not pretend to be anything else. A chair is a chair. A window is a window. 

When I sit down to write, I try to make the room that honest. I clear the table. I put the phone face down. I turn off the overhead light and use the small desk lamp that makes a warm pool around the keyboard. It is a ritual, not because I believe in rituals, but because the body needs a signal. Sit. Breathe. Start. The first sentence is always the hardest because it is the first time you admit you want something from the page. You are not just passing time. You want a thought to stay.

I think about people who have written for 2500 words without stopping. Journalists on deadline, students pulling an all-nighter, novelists in the middle of a chapter they didn’t plan. There is a particular kind of fatigue that comes from that length. It is not physical exhaustion so much as a thinning. The mind gets less careful. It starts to repeat itself. It starts to say the same thing in different words. And sometimes that repetition is useful. It tells you what you really care about.

I care about the idea that freedom is not the same as emptiness. To write freely about whatever you want is not to have nothing to say. It is to have so many things you want to say that you have to choose. Choice is the difficult part. The blank page is not blank. It is crowded with possibilities. The dog sleeping on the rug. The smell of rain from earlier today that still hangs in the curtains. The email I didn’t send. The argument I rehearsed in the shower. The memory of my grandfather’s hands. All of them are waiting.

So I pick one and I follow it. Today I am following the idea of a city at 3 a.m. There is a particular stillness at 3 a.m. that feels almost holy. The streetlights hum. A delivery truck passes and its brakes sigh. Somewhere a refrigerator cycles on. People are asleep, but the city is not. It is breathing shallowly, keeping watch over itself. If you stand on a corner at that hour you can feel how thin the veil is between the world we build and the world that simply is.

I remember being a teenager and walking home from a late movie with my friend Maya. We were 16 and convinced we were insomniacs by nature. We walked through the downtown because it was easier than taking the bus. The storefronts were dark and reflective, like mirrors. We saw ourselves in them, stretched and doubled. Maya said she liked the night because no one expected anything from her. I said I liked it because I could finally hear myself think. We were both right. The night gives you permission to be a version of yourself that is less edited.

Writing is like that too. The first draft is 3 a.m. You don’t worry about what sounds good. You worry about what is true. Later you can edit. Later you can put on the coat and go out in daylight. But the first draft is the walk home with your friend when you are both tired and honest.

There is a temptation, when you are given a prompt like write freely for 2500 words, to fill it with noise. To describe everything. To be exhaustive. But exhaustion is not the same as depth. I have read essays that are 2500 words and felt like I had learned nothing, and I have read postcards that taught me how to live. Length is a container. It does not guarantee content.

What I want in these words is a kind of movement. I want to start somewhere specific and then let the specifics lead me outward. The lamp on my desk. The way the light makes a yellow circle. The way my shadow falls across the wall. From there I can go to the idea of shadows in general, how we carry them with us, how they grow longer as the day ends. From there I can go to the idea of days ending. From there I can go to the people who never get a day that ends properly because they work night shifts or because grief keeps them awake.

This is the freedom the prompt offers. Not to be clever. To be curious. To follow a thread until it frays.

I think about my mother making tea in the kitchen while the radio played softly in the background. She would hum without realizing it. She hummed the same three notes over and over. It wasn’t a song. It was a placeholder for a song she had forgotten. I think about how much of life is placeholders. We say “I’m fine” when we are not. We say “I’ll call you back” when we know we won’t. We write “etc.” when we are tired of listing. Placeholders are a kindness. They keep the structure standing while we figure out the real thing.

Maybe writing is a way of replacing placeholders with real things. You write “she was sad” and you realize that is a placeholder. You need the specific kind of sad. The sad that makes your throat close when you smell oranges. The sad that makes you want to clean the house at midnight. The sad that sits in the kitchen and drinks cold tea.

I have been thinking a lot about time lately. Not in an abstract way. In a very literal way. How long does it take to write 2500 words? If you type 60 words per minute, about 42 minutes. If you pause to think, maybe two hours. If you write and delete, maybe four. Time expands when you are paying attention. A five-minute walk can feel like an hour if you notice every leaf. A two-hour conversation can feel like five minutes if you are fully inside it.

This is why I like writing by hand sometimes. The friction slows me down. The pen catches on the paper. My wrist aches. I cannot produce 2500 words in an hour. I might produce 400 and feel like they are real. There is a trade-off between speed and weight.

Freedom also means you can choose the pace. You can sprint and you can linger. You can write a sentence and then sit with it for twenty minutes. You can write ten sentences and then cross them all out. The page allows for that. The page does not judge your inefficiency. It just waits.

I think about the people who will read this, if anyone does. I imagine someone reading on a phone on a train. The screen is small. The words scroll by. They are tired. They are looking for something to hold onto. Maybe they are looking for permission to write badly. To write without a plan. To write about the lamp on their desk.

I want to give them that permission. The best writing advice I ever received was: write the first draft as if no one will ever see it. Then write the second draft as if everyone will. Most people never get past the first part because they are afraid of being seen. But the freedom is in the first draft. That is where you get to be messy. That is where you get to say things you don’t fully understand yet.

There is a particular pleasure in a long sentence that keeps going because you are not sure where it is going, but you trust it. It is like walking without a map. You are not lost. You are exploring. You can always come back. You can always mark the path.

I think about my father’s workshop. He had a workbench covered in tools, each in its place. He was a man of order. He would not tolerate a messy bench. Yet when he worked on something he loved, the bench would get covered in shavings and oil and little bits of metal. He would work for hours and not clean up. At the end, he would sigh and put everything back. I think writing is like that. You make a mess on purpose so something can be made. Then you clean up for the next time.

The longer you write, the more you learn about your own patterns. I tend to return to water. Rivers, rain, bathtubs, tears, oceans. I tend to return to hands. Hands doing things. Hands holding things. Hands letting go. I tend to return to light. Morning light, afternoon light, the light from a screen at night. These are my obsessions. They are not deep mysteries. They are just what catches my eye.

If I were to write a book, it would be about catching. About how we catch moments, like catching a ball, and then what we do with them once we have them. Do we throw them away? Do we keep them on a shelf? Do we try to make them into something else?

This is a long way of saying that writing freely is not the same as writing without care. It is writing with care, but without a pre-approved subject. It is allowing the subject to choose you.

I have a friend who keeps a notebook where he writes down one true sentence a day. Not a good sentence. A true one. Sometimes it is “I was angry at the barista for no reason.” Sometimes it is “I miss the smell of my childhood house after it rained.” Over years, that notebook becomes a map of an inner life. He says it is the only honest thing he has ever done.

I want that kind of honesty here. So here is a true sentence: I am aware of the time passing while I write this. I am aware that I have a cup of coffee that is now cold. I am aware that my back hurts from sitting too long. These are small truths, but they anchor the bigger ones.

Writing is a way of making the invisible visible. We carry so much inside that never gets spoken. The small grievances, the small joys, the small observations that feel too trivial to mention. But they are the material. The world is made of small things.

I think about the way a city smells in different seasons. In spring, it smells like wet concrete and cut grass. In summer, it smells like hot asphalt and sunscreen. In fall, it smells like leaves and woodsmoke. In winter, it smells like nothing, just cold. Those smells are stories. If you pay attention, you can tell where you are and when you are.

Memory works like that too. It is not a video recording. It is a smell, a texture, a fragment of a song. You cannot force it. You can only create the conditions for it to surface. A quiet room. A slow pace. A willingness to be bored.

Boredom is underrated. We are taught to fear it. We fill every moment with stimulation. But boredom is where the mind goes to work without supervision. It is where it connects things that do not seem connected. It is where it finds the thread.

So I am going to sit with boredom for a while. I am going to let the sentences come slowly. I am going to let them be imperfect. I am going to let them wander.

There is a story I have never told properly about a summer when I was twelve and I stole a library book and kept it for three months because I was afraid to return it late. The book was about a boy who lived in a lighthouse. I read it by flashlight under my covers. When I finally returned it, I was shaking. The librarian stamped it back in and said, “Good choice.” I have never forgotten that. It taught me that small acts of love can be terrifying.

I think about how many books we never return. How many ideas we borrow and never give back. How many people we owe a thank you to. The world is full of overdue returns.

Maybe writing is a way of returning something. You take an experience, you hold it, you turn it over in your hands, and then you put it back into the world in a different form. It is not the same as the original. It is changed by you. That is okay.

I want to end this with a sentence that feels like a door opening rather than a door closing. Not a conclusion, because conclusions are a kind of lie. We do not really conclude. We just pause. We stop writing because we have to stop, not because we are done.

The lamp is still on. The room is still quiet. The words are still moving. There is always more to say, and that is the comfort of it. You never run out. You only choose to stop for now.

If you have read this far, thank you. You have been a good companion for a long walk. I hope you found something here that felt familiar. I hope you felt a little more free to write your own 2500 words about whatever you want. The page is waiting. It has been waiting all along.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
I want to talk about the way light behaves in the late afternoon, because that is the thing that has stayed with me longest and because it is a good excuse to sit down and write 2500 words about nothing in particular. The sun is lower then, and it stops trying to be impressive. It is not blinding you anymore. It is horizontal, tired in a kind of generous way, and it slides across surfaces the way a hand might rest on a table.

It gets into the cracks of the city. It finds the brick between buildings that you never look at directly, and it makes that brick glow as if it had been waiting. The air is thicker. It smells like heat leaving. On days when it has rained in the morning, the asphalt still holds a faint steam, and the light catches it and turns the street into something briefly, impossibly clean.

I was thinking about this because I was asked to write. Not about anything specific. Just to write. For 2500 words. That is a strange request, and a kind one. It is permission to wander.

I live in a house with a kitchen window that faces west. In the summer the light comes in around four o'clock and it makes a rectangle on the floor. The rectangle moves. If I stand still in it, I am warm. If I move out of it, I am cool again. My cat knows this. She will arrange herself in the rectangle and then, when the rectangle moves off her, she will sigh and relocate, always with the same mild reproach, as if I had done something to the sun.

Children understand this better than adults. They will chase the patch of light across a room, or lie down in it and stare up at the ceiling, or try to trap it in a jar. I used to think it was a kind of magic, and I still do. There is no better proof that the world is made of attention. Light is only light. The room is only a room. But when they meet, something else happens.

Writing is similar. You put words down and you wait to see what happens where they meet the day. Sometimes nothing. Sometimes a rectangle of warmth appears and you sit in it for a while.

I have been reading a lot about memory lately, not in books so much as in the way my own memory keeps returning to the same few scenes and repainting them. The memory of my grandfather’s workshop, for instance. It was a small shed behind his house, with a single bulb hanging from the ceiling and a bench covered in oil. The light in there was always yellow and always a little dusty. He would work on small engines, taking them apart until they were a collection of shiny parts laid out in order, like a puzzle. He never lost a part. He had a way of knowing where everything belonged.

I remember the smell of metal and cutting oil and the faint sound of the radio playing in the next room. I remember sitting on a stool that was too tall for me and watching his hands move. They were big hands, scarred, with grease under the nails that never really came out. He would talk to me while he worked, not directly, but in a low voice, as if he were talking to the engine. “You have to listen,” he said once. “They tell you what they need if you’re patient.”

I didn’t understand then. I understand it now in a different way. Writing is like that. You have to listen to the sentence. You have to be patient with it. You can’t force it to work. You can try to, and you’ll get something, but it will be tight and it will hurt.

My grandfather died when I was seventeen. The workshop was cleared out. I took a small wooden mallet he had made from a piece of oak and a worn screwdriver with a black handle. The rest went to someone else. I sometimes wonder if the shed is still there. I think it probably isn’t. The house was sold. The new owners likely needed the space for a garden. It is a reasonable thought.

But I still have the memory of the light in there, and the way it made the metal parts look like they were alive. That memory is not accurate. I know it isn’t. Memory never is. It is a reconstruction. It is a story we tell ourselves about a story we told ourselves earlier. The light was probably not that good. The workshop was probably cold in the winter and stifling in the summer. But the memory has become a place I can go back to when I need to be quiet.

That is one of the things I love about language. It lets you build rooms you can return to. You can furnish them with whatever you need. You can leave the windows open or closed.

There is a park near where I used to live. It had a big oak tree in the middle of it, and a bench underneath it that faced away from the playground. People would sit there with coffee and newspapers. In the fall the leaves would fall and pile up around the bench, and no one would clean them up for weeks. The oak would drop acorns with a soft thud. Sometimes a squirrel would run up and down the trunk, and you could watch it for a long time without getting bored.

I would go there after school. I would do my homework on that bench. I would watch the light move across the grass. I remember one afternoon in particular because it rained lightly and then stopped, and the sun came out and everything smelled like wet earth. A woman walked her dog, and the dog stopped to sniff at the base of the oak, and the woman laughed and said, “He’s writing a novel about the tree.” I laughed too, but I thought about it later. It is a nice idea, that animals are writing novels about us, in their own way.

The park is gone now. They built apartments there. I walk past sometimes and I can still see the oak in my mind, and I can still feel the bench under me. The apartments are nice, I suppose. People need places to live. But the oak is not there. I have photos, but photos are not the same. Photos are proof, not presence.

We spend so much of our lives trying to hold onto presence. We take pictures, we write notes, we keep objects. The mallet, the screwdriver. The rectangle of light on the floor. We think if we can just capture it, we won’t lose it.

But we always lose it. That is the nature of things. The light moves. The seasons change. The people we love get older and then they are gone. You can’t stop it. You can only notice it as it happens. That is the work.

I think about the people who have lived in the houses I have lived in. Before me and after me. The walls have heard other voices. The kitchen has seen other hands. There is a particular kind of humility in that. You are a temporary resident. You are a caretaker for a while.

When I move out, someone else will sit at the table I sit at. They will look out the same window. The light will come in at four o’clock and make the same rectangle on the floor. They will have their own cat, or they won’t. They will have their own memories. The house will accumulate them, layer by layer, like varnish.

This is why I like old houses. You can feel the layers. The paint that has been painted over. The floorboards that have been worn down in certain spots. The way a door sticks in the summer and swings freely in the winter. It is a record of use. It is a kind of writing.

We are all writing, constantly, with our bodies, with our choices, with the small things we leave behind. A coffee ring on a table. A scratch on a windowsill. A plant that was loved and then forgotten.

I have a plant. It is a pothos. It grows slowly, and it is very forgiving. I forget to water it for weeks and it just droops a little and then perks up again when I remember. It is a good teacher. It doesn’t demand attention, it just asks for consistency. I like that.

In the late afternoon, the light comes through the kitchen window and hits the pothos, and the leaves turn a kind of translucent green. You can see the veins. It is beautiful in a quiet way. It doesn’t need to be beautiful. It just is.

I think about how many people have sat in the late afternoon light and felt something shift inside them, something softening. It is not a revelation, usually. It is not a lightning bolt. It is a small loosening. A remembering.

Sometimes I think the world is too loud. The notifications, the alerts, the endless scroll. It is hard to hear yourself think. But the late afternoon light is quiet. It doesn’t ask anything of you. It just arrives.

If I could give anyone one piece of advice, it would be to sit in that light for five minutes a day and do nothing. Don’t read, don’t scroll, don’t make a to-do list. Just sit. Feel the warmth on your skin. Watch the dust move in the air. Listen to the house settle.

It sounds simple, and it is. That is the trick of it. The simple things are the hardest to remember to do.

I have a friend who keeps a notebook by her bed. She writes one sentence a day. Not a journal, not a diary. Just one sentence. Sometimes it is, “The rain sounded like paper.” Sometimes it is, “I missed my mother today.” Sometimes it is, “I am tired.” She says it helps her feel like she is still here, like she is still paying attention.

I started doing that a few months ago. My notebook is messy. The handwriting gets worse as the night goes on. Some days I write a full page. Some days I write nothing. It doesn’t matter. The point is the return. The point is the habit of noticing.

Writing 2500 words on demand is not a habit, it is a sprint. But it is also a kind of noticing. You have to keep going, you have to keep finding the next sentence. You have to stay with it.

Sometimes the sentences come easily. Sometimes they feel like dragging a boulder. Both are fine. Both are part of it.

I wonder what the person who asked for this will do with it. Maybe they will read it all the way through. Maybe they will skim. Maybe they will never read it at all. That is okay too. The writing is its own event. It exists whether or not it is witnessed.

I think about the idea of freedom in writing. Free writing is not the same as careless writing. It is still work. It requires attention. You have to be free enough to follow a thought without judging it, but disciplined enough to keep going when the thought runs out.

That is what I am trying to do here. I am trying to stay with the day. I am trying to stay with the light.

The kettle is whistling in the kitchen. I should probably get up and make tea. But I want to stay here a little longer, in this rectangle of light, with these words.

If you are reading this, thank you for being here with me. I don’t know you, but you are sharing this space for a moment. That is enough.

I will end with an image. It is of a small boat on a lake at dusk. The water is glassy. The sky is pink and blue. The boat is still. No one is in it. It is just there, floating, being held up by the water. That is how I want to feel at the end of a day of writing. Held up. Still. Ready to float.

And the light will come again tomorrow, at four o’clock, and it will make another rectangle on the floor. And I will sit in it, if I remember to.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
The first thing you notice about the house on Alder Street is that it never quite shuts up. Not in the way a house with loud appliances shuts up, but in the way a house that has been lived in for eighty years keeps a low, continuous hum in its bones. The pipes sigh when the heat kicks on at 5:47 a.m. The second floor settles with a soft exhale around midnight. The refrigerator in the kitchen has a particular tick, three ticks, pause, tick, that I have come to recognize as a kind of Morse code for "I am still here."

I moved in last winter because the rent was cheap and the landlord was kind in the way that elderly landlords are kind when they have no children and a spare key they keep forgetting to return. The walls are thin enough that I can hear the woman across the hall hum while she waters her plants. The man downstairs practices the same four bars of a Chopin nocturne on a digital piano with the sustain pedal stuck down. I have learned their schedules by sound.

For the first month I tried to make the house quiet. I bought earplugs, a white noise machine, a thick rug. The rug only made the footsteps louder because now they were muffled and therefore more intentional. The white noise machine sounded like an airplane that was always taking off. The earplugs made my own blood loud.

So I stopped fighting it. I started listening.

That is how I ended up writing at 3 a.m. Not because I am nocturnal, though I am, but because 3 a.m. is the hour when the house is most honest. The hum goes down a register. The pipes stop. The hum of the street outside thins to the occasional truck. The neighbor's plants are dry. The pianist sleeps.

At 3 a.m. the room becomes a small, clean thing. The desk lamp pools a warm circle on the wood. My laptop is open but I do not type for a long time. I sit. I wait for the first sentence to arrive, and I have learned that the first sentence never arrives if I demand it. It arrives when I am not looking for it, when I am thinking about the way the radiator knocks or the way my coffee went cold two hours ago.

Writing freely, I have come to understand, is not the same as writing well. It is not the same as writing at all, really. It is a posture. It is an agreement you make with yourself that you will not stop at the first sign of embarrassment. You will not edit while you are making. You will not ask, "Is this good?" until the room is full of words and you have to decide what to do with them.

I think about my grandmother, who wrote letters every Sunday for fifty-two years. Not emails, not texts. Letters on lined paper with a blue ballpoint pen that she kept in the pocket of her cardigan. She wrote to my mother, who lived three towns over, about the weather, about the price of tomatoes, about the church bake sale, about a dream she had where her own mother was still alive and young. She wrote about everything and nothing. She wrote because the week had to be accounted for somewhere outside her head.

I have a box of those letters in the closet. The paper is yellowing at the edges. The ink has faded in places where her hand pressed too hard. I read them sometimes when I cannot write. They are not literature. They are not even particularly interesting, if you are being cruel. But they are honest in a way that is rare. She never wrote to impress. She wrote to continue.

That is the thing I keep returning to when I sit in the quiet at 3 a.m. and the cursor blinks. The cursor blinks like a small animal waiting to be fed. I want to feed it something real, not something clever. Cleverness is easy. Cleverness is a performance. Realness is harder because it requires you to admit that you do not know what you think you know.

I used to think writing was about having something to say. Now I think writing is about discovering that you have something you didn't know you were saying. The first draft is a conversation with a part of yourself that is less articulate, more scared, more honest. It stutters. It repeats. It goes off on tangents about the refrigerator tick. It remembers the way the light falls on the kitchen table at 4 p.m. in October.

I have a notebook where I write down those tangents. "The way the bus driver at the 7:15 always nods but never makes eye contact." "The smell of the laundromat on Thursdays, which is mostly fabric softener and old pennies." "The man who walks his three dogs in a triangle formation, as if they are a geometry problem he is trying to solve." These are not stories. They are scraps. But scraps are where stories start.

One night last spring I wrote for three hours straight about a pigeon that had gotten into the building's stairwell. It was a ridiculous subject. The pigeon was gray and a little wet. It kept trying to fly up but the ceiling was low and the fluorescent light buzzed. I wrote about its wings, about the way it looked at me with one beady eye, about the way I felt guilty for watching it instead of helping it. I wrote about my own father, who loved pigeons, who kept a pair in a coop behind the garage when I was seven. I wrote about how I had never told anyone that.

When I finished, I read it back and thought, "This is nonsense." But it was not nonsense. It was the first honest thing I had written in months because it had no agenda. It was not trying to be a poem or an essay or a viral post. It was just trying to stay with something until it made sense.

That is freedom, I think. Not freedom from structure or grammar or taste. Freedom from the need to be finished. Freedom from the need to be good. Freedom from the audience that lives in your head, the one that looks like your high school English teacher and your ex and your own voice when you are tired.

I have tried to build a small ritual around that freedom. A glass of water. The lamp on. Phone in another room. Five minutes of staring at the wall. Then, no matter what, I write one sentence. Just one. It can be terrible. It can be "I don't know what to write." That counts. Usually, once the first sentence is down, the second one is easier. The third one is easier still. By the tenth sentence, I am no longer thinking about writing. I am thinking about the thing.

Sometimes the thing is the house. Sometimes the thing is the pigeon. Sometimes the thing is the memory of my grandmother's kitchen, where the radio was always on low and she hummed along off-key and the linoleum was cool under bare feet. I can still feel that coolness in the summer. I can still smell the dish soap she used, which was a cheap lemon kind that left my hands squeaky.

I think about how much of our lives we spend trying to translate experience into something legible. We take the hum of a house and try to make it a metaphor. We take the tick of a refrigerator and try to make it a rhythm. We want meaning, and we are so hungry for it that we will manufacture it if we have to.

But sometimes meaning arrives without us manufacturing it. It arrives in the quiet, in the space between the ticks. It arrives when you stop trying to write about the pigeon and you just write the pigeon.

I have been keeping a document for six months now that is just a long, unbroken stream of this. No titles. No chapters. No paragraphs, really, just line breaks when I get up to pee. It is 80,000 words of me talking to myself about the bus, about the weather, about the way my sister laughs when she is nervous, about the dream where I am back in school and I have no pants on. It is messy. It contradicts itself. It is the most alive thing I have ever made.

People ask me what I am writing. I say, "I don't know." They look disappointed. They want a book, a project, a purpose. I want a room where I can be honest without having to justify it. I want the freedom to be unfinished.

The house on Alder Street is getting louder again. It's 5:47. The heat is kicking on. The pipes sigh. Somewhere across the hall a plant is being watered. The pianist is still asleep, but his digital piano will wake up later, and the same four bars will play again. The refrigerator ticks three times, pauses, ticks.

I should get up soon. I have work. I have emails. The world will ask me for things again.

But for now, the cursor is still blinking. The lamp is still warm. The room is still quiet enough to hear myself think. And I am still here, writing freely, because I finally understood that the point was never to produce something perfect. The point was to stay in the room long enough for the house to tell me its stories, and to be brave enough to write them down exactly as they sound.

If you ever find yourself at 3 a.m. with a blank page and a ticking refrigerator, do not try to be brilliant. Just start. Write the tick. Write the pause. Write the way the light looks on the wood. Write the fear that you are wasting your time. Write it all. The rest will come, or it won't, and either way, you will have been honest for a little while, which is more than most of us get.

I am going to save this and close the laptop. The sun will be up soon, and the house will get loud again. But I will know that somewhere in the quiet, I was here, and I was listening, and I was writing.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
I was asked to write freely about whatever I want for 2500 words, and the first honest thing that comes to mind is that I am aware of the number. 2500 words. It sits there like a small stone in the palm of the mind. You can feel its weight. You can try to ignore it, but you know it is there, counting along with you, and that awareness changes the freedom. True freedom would be to write until the thought stops, not until the word count ends. But here I am, negotiating with a number.

The request itself is a kind of kindness. Write about whatever you want. No topic, no thesis, no audience to impress. Just permission. Most days I don't get permission to be unfocused. Most days writing has a job: explain, persuade, summarize, solve. This is different. This is a room with the lights left on and nobody waiting for me to leave.

So I will take you to the kitchen at 2:17 a.m. in a house I used to live in. The refrigerator hums in a key I never learned to name. There is a chipped mug on the counter with a thin film of old coffee at the bottom. I am not there now, I am here, but the memory is so tactile that my tongue finds the taste of that coffee, slightly burnt, slightly sweet from the sugar I added too late. I was awake because I had read something that unsettled me and then I had a thought about how unsettledness is a kind of alertness, and I wanted to follow it until it became something else.

That is what free writing is, I think. You follow a thread not because you know where it leads, but because you want to see what you can pull out with it. Sometimes you pull out a sweater. Sometimes you pull out a knot. Sometimes you pull out nothing but the feeling of having pulled.

I think about the people who write for a living and how rarely they get to write without a destination. Even a diary has a destination: the self. A novel has characters who demand consistency. An essay has an argument. Here the argument is just: keep going. Keep going is not nothing. It is a discipline of attention. You have to stay with the sentence when it gets boring. You have to stay with the image when it gets embarrassing. You have to stay with the same room in your head long enough for the wallpaper to peel.

The wallpaper in this room is made of all the things I have been told to remember. The capital of Mongolia is Ulaanbaatar. Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius at sea level. My first phone number. The names of the streets on my block in the order I learned them as a child, as if they were beads on a string. I can recite them without trying, and sometimes I wonder why some things get stored so efficiently and others evaporate the moment I need them, like the name of a song I heard in a grocery store last Tuesday.

Maybe memory is not a library. Maybe it is a city. Some neighborhoods are well lit and you can walk them without a map. Others are dark and you only find them when you are lost. The kitchen at 2:17 a.m. is a well lit neighborhood. I can walk there whenever I want. The year I turned nineteen and the apartment with the radiator that clanked like a metronome is a street I avoid because it is damp. The smell of the laundry room in my grandmother's house is a small square park where I always sit for a while.

If I were to map my mind with the honesty that this prompt allows, I would draw a lot of parks and very few main roads. I am good at lingering. I am bad at arriving. That is why the idea of writing 2500 words feels both generous and cruel. Generous because it says stay, linger, look around. Cruel because it eventually says stop.

I wonder about the people who read this. Will there be one? Will there be a thousand? Does it matter? The impulse to write freely assumes a reader who is also free, someone who will read without demanding a point. That is a rare reader. Most readers want a handle. They want to know why they should keep going. I can offer them only this: I am keeping going because I was asked to, and because I am curious what happens if I don't edit myself for a while.

So let me tell you about the train. There is a commuter train I used to take that ran along a river. In the winter the river was gray and still. In the spring it was high and fast and full of ice that moved like slow animals. I would stand at the same window every morning and watch the same trees pass, and yet I never saw the same trees twice because light changes them, and because I changed. One morning I noticed a heron standing in the shallows. It stood so still I thought it was a post. Then it moved its head, a quick snap, and caught something. I watched it swallow.
