The whole thing took three seconds. I have never seen that heron again, but I have thought about it for years. That is how memory works. It freezes the three seconds and lets the rest of the ride blur.

We are all collecting herons. We are all collecting moments that don't fit into the story we tell about our lives but that we keep anyway because they feel true in a way the story does not. The kitchen at 2:17 a.m. is not an important moment. Nothing happened there. I didn't solve a problem or have a breakthrough. I just existed in a room with a humming refrigerator. And yet it is more real to me than many important moments.

Perhaps importance is overrated. Perhaps the small, unproductive moments are the ones that hold us together. The walk to the mailbox. The way the light hits the kitchen table at 4 p.m. in October. The sound of a neighbor practicing piano badly and then getting one measure right. These are the stitches.

If I could give you one piece of advice from the freewriting experiment I am conducting right now, it would be this: pay attention to the stitches. The big moments will get their own monuments. The small moments will not. You have to keep them yourself.

I am thinking about the word free. Free as in no cost. Free as in liberated. Free as in able to move without restriction. All of those meanings are true here. This writing is free because no one is paying me for it, and no one is telling me what to say, and I can move my attention wherever it wants to go. That freedom is not empty. It is full. It is full of detritus. It is full of the kitchen mug and the heron and the radiator and the laundry room smell.

It is also full of anxiety. Because when you are free, you have to choose. And choice is heavy. I could write about philosophy. I could write about love. I could write about the way my hands look when I type, the way the knuckles are a little swollen at the end of the day. I could write about the future, about the planet warming, about the news that never stops coming. I could write about the past, about my mother humming while she cooked, about the first book I ever finished and how I felt like I had climbed a mountain.

All of these are available. All of these are waiting. The difficulty is not finding something to say. The difficulty is letting something be enough.

Maybe that is the real lesson of writing 2500 words on a whim. You learn that enough is a moving target. At 500 words you think you are done. At 1000 you think you have said it all. At 1500 you realize you have only warmed up. At 2000 you start to feel tired in the way you feel tired after a long walk, pleasantly exhausted. At 2300 you start to search for a way to end gracefully, and you realize there is no graceful end, only a stopping.

So I will stop at some point that feels approximate. I will stop not because I have finished thinking, but because the stone in my palm has reached the weight I was asked to carry.

I want to leave you with an image. It is the kitchen at 2:17 a.m. again, but now the light is on. The refrigerator hums. The mug is chipped. The coffee is cold. And I am sitting at the table, writing in a notebook, not because I have to, but because I am awake and the night is quiet and there is nothing else to do but be with myself for a while. That is what this was. That is what this is.

Thank you for asking me to write freely. I will keep the room lit for a little longer.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
I started writing this at 3:47 p.m. on a Tuesday because the kettle whistled and I didn’t want to get up. The kitchen was warm in the way kitchens are warm in late summer, when the heat of the day has finally sunk into the walls and is now radiating back out at you slowly, like an apology. I had a mug with a chip in the rim that I’ve been meaning to throw away for three years. It holds the tea perfectly. That’s the thing about flaws; they become part of the ritual.

Outside the window, the street was doing what streets do when nobody is paying attention to them. A delivery van idled for too long at the corner and then left. A woman in a yellow raincoat walked a dog that was too big for its leash. A boy on a scooter tried to do a trick he couldn’t do and nearly took out the newspaper stand. None of it was important, but all of it was happening at once, and I was sitting in a chair with a blank page open and the vague sense that I had been asked to do something impossible: write freely for a long time.

Freely. What a strange word to use about writing. It implies a kind of permission that you have to give yourself first. No outline. No thesis. No point. Just the movement of the hand, the sound of the keys, the accumulation of sentences like stones you pick up while walking along a riverbank. You don’t know why you’re picking them up. You just know you want something to carry.

I think about the people who lived in this house before me. There’s a faint pencil mark on the back of the bedroom closet door, a height chart from 1987 to 1999. A boy grew up here. At 12 he was 4’11”. At 16 he was 5’9”. Then it stops. Did he leave? Did he die? Did he just stop caring about being measured? I like to imagine him coming home from school with a backpack full of books he didn’t read, putting his shoes in the same place every night, learning the exact spot on the kitchen floor where the linoleum is cold even in July. Those small cartographies are what make a house a home, and then they are erased.

The library on 4th Street has a smell I can’t describe without sounding like a cliché. Old paper and lemon cleaner and the faint metallic tang of the microfilm machines that nobody uses anymore. I went there last winter because the heat was broken at my apartment and I needed a place to be warm that wasn’t a coffee shop. I sat at a table in the back near the biography section and read about someone else’s life for three hours. It was comforting. The biography was about a botanist who spent forty years cataloguing mosses. She never discovered a new species. She just described the ones she found more carefully than anyone else had. The last line of the book said, “She died in her garden, surrounded by specimens she had never named.” I underlined it. I still don’t know why.

Writing is like that sometimes. You are not trying to be the first. You are trying to be more careful. To notice the way light falls on a chipped mug at 3:47 p.m. To remember that the boy on the scooter had a blue helmet with a sticker of a dinosaur on the back. To record the exact pitch of the kettle’s whistle, which is higher than it used to be because the heating element is wearing out.

I have a theory that everyone has a private inventory of small, unremarkable facts that they keep because nobody else would want them. The number of steps from the front door to the mailbox is 37. The bus that comes at 7:12 is always three minutes late on Wednesdays. My grandmother’s favorite song was “Moon River” and she would hum it while shelling peas, and the peas would be warm from the sun. I know the color of the grout between the tiles in the bathroom of the house I lived in when I was nine. It was a beige that was not quite beige.

If you write freely, you start pulling that inventory out. It spills. It is messy. It is not impressive. That’s the point.

I once met a man at a train station who told me he collected the paperclips that people left on the tables in waiting rooms. He had a shoebox full of them. Different shapes, different metals. He could tell you which station each one came from by the rust pattern. “People drop them when they’re in a hurry,” he said. “Or when they’re finished with something and they don’t care about it anymore.” He wasn’t sad about it. He was reverent. He thought each paperclip was a little act of abandonment, a tiny confession that someone had let go.

That’s what I want to do with these words. Let go of them.

The afternoon is moving. The light has shifted an inch to the left. The tea is cooling. I can hear the neighbor’s television through the wall, a laugh track from a show that ended a decade ago. Somewhere a cat is yowling, not in distress, just announcing itself. The street outside is quieter now. The delivery van is gone. The woman with the dog is gone. The boy with the scooter is probably home eating something he was told not to eat before dinner.

I think about time as a substance. It accumulates in corners. In the dust on top of the bookshelf. In the way your knees feel after you’ve been sitting too long. You can’t see it moving, but you can feel its weight. When you write for a long time without stopping, you start to feel that weight lift a little. The sentences become a place to put the excess. You are not creating meaning so much as you are clearing space.

There is a Japanese word, *komorebi*, for the sunlight that filters through the leaves of trees. It is a specific kind of light, dappled and moving. You can’t photograph it properly because by the time you lift the camera, it’s gone. That’s what free writing is for me. It’s an attempt to catch the komorebi of the mind. The flickering thoughts that appear when you are not trying to catch them. The half-formed memory of a smell. The sudden understanding that you are lonely in a way you haven’t admitted to yourself all day.

I am not lonely right now. I am sitting with a kettle and a chipped mug and a window and a street. I am in company with all the things I can see. That is enough.

If I keep writing, the words will start to repeat. I will say “the” too many times. I will circle back to the same anecdote. I will describe the chip in the mug from three different angles. That’s okay. Repetition is a form of attention. When you repeat something, you are saying: look, this matters enough for me to say it again.

The boy’s height marks in the closet. The botanist with the mosses. The man with the paperclips. The komorebi. The kettle. The chipped mug. The 37 steps to the mailbox. The blue helmet with the dinosaur sticker. The beige grout. The woman in the yellow raincoat. All of these things are true. None of them are connected in any logical way. But they are connected by me, by the fact that I am noticing them in the same afternoon, in the same kitchen, with the same slightly bitter tea.

That is the only connection we ever really have. The through-line of a single consciousness moving through time, picking up stones.

I wonder what the boy who grew up in this house would think if he came back now. Would he recognize the kitchen? Would he notice the new faucet? Would he see the height marks and feel a pang? Maybe he would stand in the doorway and listen to the way the house breathes at 3:47 p.m. The refrigerator hums. The pipes tick. The floor creaks under the weight of the chair. He might feel, for a moment, that he is still here. That’s the strange mercy of places. They hold our ghosts lightly.

Writing freely is a way of being a good host to those ghosts. You don’t interrogate them. You don’t try to make them speak in complete sentences. You just make room at the table. You put out tea.

The sun is lower now. The light is amber. It makes the dust motes visible. They are always there, but you only see them when the light is right. I think that’s a metaphor for something, but I’m too tired to figure out what. Maybe it’s just dust.

I have been writing for a while. My fingers are stiff. The tea is cold. The chip in the mug catches my lip when I drink. I should get up and make more tea. But if I get up, the spell will break. The page will be finished. The afternoon will be over. So I stay.

There is a kind of freedom in not finishing. In not needing to arrive. In letting the sentences wander like the dog on the too-short leash, pulling a little, pausing, sniffing at things.

I think about the people who will read this, if anyone does. They will skim. They will look for the point. There is no point. There is just this: a man in a kitchen with a chipped mug, watching the light move, remembering a botanist, a boy, a paperclip collector, a woman in yellow. That is the whole story. The rest is commentary.

Maybe that’s enough.

The kettle is silent now. The street is quiet. The neighbor’s television has switched to the news. I can hear a siren far away, dopplering past. The cat has stopped yowling. The boy with the scooter is gone.

I am still here. The page is still open. The words are still coming, slower now, but they are coming. They are not good. They are not bad. They are just present.

And presence, I think, is the most radical thing you can offer in a world that is always telling you to be productive, to be concise, to be impressive. To sit in a kitchen at 3:47 p.m. and write about a chipped mug for 2500 words is a small act of rebellion. It says: I am here. This matters. The dust motes in the amber light matter. The height marks on the closet door matter. The moss that was never named matters.

If you keep writing, you will eventually run out of things to say. That is the moment when you start to say the real things. The things you didn’t know you knew. The things you’ve been carrying in your pockets like smooth stones.

I have a smooth stone in my pocket from a beach I visited when I was twenty. I don’t know why I kept it. It’s just a stone. But it is warm when I hold it. It fits my palm exactly.

That’s what I want these words to be. Warm. Fitted. Unnecessary.

I think I am almost done. The light is almost gone. The kitchen is turning blue. The tea has been cold for a long time. The chip in the mug is still there.

I will stop soon. But not yet.

One more sentence. Then another. Then another.

Because the afternoon is still here, and I am still writing, and that is enough.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
I was asked to write freely about whatever I want for 2500 words, and for a long time I stared at the blank page the way you stare at an empty kitchen when you have no groceries, wondering if freedom is a kind of hunger. If I can write about anything, then what is the thing? The thing is always the same. It is the small, stubborn inventory of a life that has been lived in rooms with light that slants in at a certain hour.

I live in a city that never quite decides if it is coastal or inland. The wind comes off the water in the morning and smells like brine and diesel. By noon it turns to dust. By evening it smells like someone cooking garlic on a fire escape three buildings over. I have lived here for nine years and I still do not know the names of the people who run the laundromat on the corner, but I know that the woman who works the evening shift always hums while she folds towels, a low tune that is half lullaby, half radio static. I know that the dryer on the left side takes longer than the dryer on the right. I know that if I come in on a Tuesday after rain, the floor is still damp near the door.

That kind of knowing is not impressive. It does not belong in a novel. It is the kind of knowing you accumulate when you are paying attention to the wrong things on purpose, because the right things are too loud.

When I was a child I believed that adults had a secret filing system inside their heads where they kept all the useful information about the world. How to fix a faucet. How to say no without sounding cruel. Where the money goes. I spent my adolescence trying to hack that system, reading manuals in the library, listening at doors. What I learned instead was that most adults are just making it up as they go, and that the filing system is mostly full of grocery lists and half-remembered apologies.

There is a particular kind of tiredness that comes from writing. It is not the tiredness of lifting or running. It is a tiredness in the jaw, in the eyes, a faint buzz behind the teeth. You sit down with the intention to say something clear and you find yourself saying something ornate because clarity feels dangerous. Clarity means you might be wrong. Ornament means you might be interesting.

I think about the people who write long things. Letters. Novels. Eulogies. They are trying to create a container large enough for a feeling that would otherwise spill all over the kitchen counter. Two thousand five hundred words is a strange container. It is not a short story. It is not an essay. It is a walk. It is enough time to leave the house, go around the block twice, notice the way the light changes, and come back again changed slightly.

My grandmother kept a notebook. It was a cheap spiral bound thing with yellow pages. She wrote in it every night for forty years. Mostly she wrote about the weather, the price of eggs, who was sick. On the back cover she had written a list of names, all the people she had ever loved. It was not a long list. There were twenty-three names. I found it after she died and I sat on the floor of her apartment for an hour with that notebook in my lap, turning the pages. There was no revelation. There was no secret. There was only the evidence of a life being tended, day by day, in small sentences.

I think about that when I am asked to write freely. Freedom is not the absence of constraints. Freedom is knowing which constraints to keep. The constraint of 2500 words is actually a kindness. It tells me I cannot explain everything. I have to choose.

I choose the bus. The 47. It runs from the industrial district up through the university and then down into the old neighborhood where the houses are narrow and painted colors that have faded to something softer than they were intended to be. I ride it most mornings because I like the way the city reveals itself in increments. First the warehouses, then the students with backpacks, then the mothers with strollers, then the men who are clearly going to work and the women who are clearly going to work and the old people who are going nowhere in particular and that is the point.

On the 47 there is a seat by the window that is slightly warmer than the rest because the heater vent is directly above it. I have claimed it as mine in the way people claim public benches. I sit there and watch the city pass. I watch the same mural of a fish on a brick wall. I watch the same dog always tied to the same lamppost, always looking up at the same window. I watch the light change on the water towers.

The driver knows the route by muscle memory. He does not look at the road so much as he feels it. He brakes at the same spot every time. He has a coffee in a travel mug with a chip in the rim. He says good morning to everyone who boards, even when it is raining. Even when it is late. I think he is the most honest person I know.

Writing is like being a bus driver. You have a route. You have stops. You can get distracted. You can take a detour. But people are relying on you to get them to where they need to go, even if they don't know it yet.

I once tried to write a book about my father. I wrote two hundred pages and then I stopped because I realized I was writing about myself with him as a backdrop. That is not a crime. Most writing is that. We write about the people we love in order to learn how to love them, or how to stop loving them, or how to forgive them for being people.

My father was a carpenter. He built things that lasted. Bookshelves, cabinets, a porch. He never wrote anything down. He kept his plans in his head. When he died, I found a drawer full of pencils, all worn down to nubs. I took one home. It still writes, faintly. The lead is soft and it makes a gray line on the page, not black. I use it sometimes when I am trying to be gentle with myself.

There is a certain melancholy to the act of counting words. It reminds you that language is made of units, and units can be measured, and measurement can feel like control. But the best sentences are the ones that refuse to be counted. They take up more space than they should. They linger.

I want to talk about the way the air smells after it rains in August. It smells like hot asphalt cooling, like the inside of a mailbox, like cut grass and something metallic. Children run out without coats. People who have been waiting for the rain come outside and stand in it. The city exhales.

I want to talk about the way people hold their phones like shields. I want to talk about the way they look up at the same time, as if a bell has rung. I want to talk about the way we have all agreed to be distracted together.

I want to talk about the small kindnesses that never make it into stories. The way the librarian at the branch on 5th will always pull a book from the hold shelf for you and leave it on the cart with your name on a sticky note. The way the man who sells pretzels at the station always gives you an extra mustard packet without you asking. The way my neighbor waters my plants when I am away and never tells me, I just come home and they are alive.

I think about time. How we think we are running out of it, and then we waste it on things that feel urgent but are not important. How 2500 words is a small amount of time. How you can read it in ten minutes. How you can write it in an afternoon if you do not stop to think.

Thinking is the problem. Thinking makes you hesitate. Thinking makes you want to make every sentence perfect. Perfection is a kind of death. It freezes the thing.

Better to write like you are talking to someone you trust. Better to let the sentences be a little loose at the edges. Better to let the handwriting be messy.

I have a friend who says she writes to remember. I write to forget. I write to get the things out of my head so they stop repeating. The difference is not important. We are both trying to make the interior livable.

There is a room in my apartment that gets the best light in the winter. It is the kitchen. The sun comes in low and hits the table at four in the afternoon and makes a square of gold on the linoleum. I sit there and drink tea and watch the light move. It moves slowly. It is always moving. If you watch it long enough you realize the light is never in the same place twice, even though it looks the same.

That is the trick of the everyday. It looks the same until you pay attention. Then it is always new.

I think about the word "freely." It implies a kind of permission. But permission is not enough. You also need a reason. Why write? Because someone asked. Because you have something to say. Because you have nothing to say and that is the same thing.

I think about the people who will read this. Maybe no one. Maybe one person on a bus. Maybe a machine. It does not matter. The writing is a room you build for a moment. You do not know who will sit in it.

I will tell you about the night the power went out. It was a summer night, hot and still. The whole block went dark. People came out onto their porches with flashlights and candles. Someone started playing guitar. Someone else brought out a cooler of beer. We sat in the dark and talked about things we never talk about when the lights are on. We talked about fear and about wanting to be better. The city was quiet without the hum of the traffic. You could hear the crickets. You could hear the river.

When the power came back, everyone went inside. It was like a dream ending. But for a little while we were free of the glow. We were free of the screens. We were just people in the dark, listening.

I want to write like that. Like people in the dark, listening.

The notebook my grandmother kept is now on my desk. I opened it to a random page. It says: "June 12. Rain. Eggs 43 cents. Maria called. She is fine." That is it. That is the whole entry. And yet in that small line there is a whole life. Rain. Eggs. A phone call. A reassurance. The mundane is holy if you let it be.

I think about the 2500 word limit and I feel a little less anxious. It is not a mountain. It is a walk. I can walk that far.

So I walk. I walk through the memory of the bus, the kitchen light, the notebook, the power outage. I walk through the laundromat and the fish mural and the dog on the lamppost. I walk through the idea that we are all trying to be kind in a world that rewards speed. I walk through the understanding that writing is not about being brilliant. It is about being present.

If you are reading this, you are present with me for a few minutes. That is enough. That is everything.

I could keep going. I could talk about the way my mother folds laundry, the way she always folds the socks in pairs and then stacks them like little bricks. I could talk about the way the first snow smells like cold and about the way the last snow smells like dirt. I could talk about the way people say goodbye at airports, the way they hold on a second too long.

But I am running out of words, and that is the point. The constraint is a gift. It tells me to stop.

I will stop here, in the kitchen light, with a cup of tea that has gone cold. The page is full. The day is still going on outside. The bus is still running. The city is still turning.

And somewhere, someone is writing freely about whatever they want, and for a moment, that is enough.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
I woke up to the sound of the refrigerator humming and realized it had been humming for years. Not just the refrigerator. The whole apartment hums. The pipes, the elevator down the hall, the traffic on the avenue three floors below, the neighbor who practices violin at 7:15 every morning and always stops at the same measure, as if she has forgotten how to finish. I lay there for a while and listened to it all, not trying to make sense of it, just letting it accumulate. That is a skill I have been practicing lately, the art of letting things accumulate without sorting them.

When I was a child I believed that every day had to be filed away. I had a shoebox under my bed with tickets, a broken tooth, a photograph of my grandmother standing in front of a house that no longer exists. I thought that if I kept everything, I would eventually understand what I was doing with my life. Now I think the opposite is true. The more I keep, the less I understand. The shoebox is now a cloud storage account with 47 gigabytes of photos I will never look at again. I still take them.

There is a bench on the corner of 5th and Mercer where I sometimes sit with a coffee that is too hot and watch people walk their dogs. The dogs are always more honest than the people. They stop, they sniff, they lie down in the sun. People walk with their eyes on their phones, or their eyes on the ground, or their eyes on nothing at all, a practiced vacancy. I have come to recognize the different kinds of walking. There is the brisk walk of someone who is late for something they do not want to be late for. There is the slow walk of someone who is waiting for a bus that will not come for twenty minutes. There is the walk of someone who has just received bad news and is trying not to cry in public. I have been all three of those people on the same Tuesday.

The city keeps changing its skin. A bodega becomes a juice bar becomes a nail salon becomes a bodega again. The signs go up in English first, then Spanish, then a language I cannot read, and then they are gone. I like to take photos of the signs before they disappear, not because I am a historian, but because I am sentimental about the moment when a place is in between identities. That in-betweenness is where everything interesting happens. It is also where everything gets torn down.

I have been thinking a lot about time. Not in a grand philosophical way, but in a very practical way. Time is the thing that makes toast burn if you look away. Time is the thing that makes a song you love feel embarrassing after a few years, and then feel like a secret again after ten. Time is the way my mother’s hands have changed. When I was small they were capable and warm. Now they shake a little when she pours tea. She pretends it is the cup, not her hands. I pretend I do not notice. We are both good at pretending.

My job involves words. I sit in front of a screen and move words around until they look like they mean something. Most days they do not. I write emails that say “just circling back” and “per your request.” I write reports that no one will read. I write descriptions for products that have no history. It is a strange kind of work, making language do labor. Sometimes I think about the people who made the words I use every day. Who first said “okay”? Who first thought to call a place “home” and a place “away”? The words feel so solid now, but they were once someone’s experiment.

In the evening I walk home through the park. The park is full of people feeding pigeons, which they are not supposed to do. The pigeons know this. They wait. In winter the park is empty except for the runners who wear too many layers and the old men who feed the pigeons anyway. In summer the park is a loud, sweaty, beautiful mess of music and children and people selling watches out of backpacks. I like both versions. I like the idea that a place can hold two opposite moods at once and not collapse.

I have a friend who collects broken things. Not valuable broken things, just broken things. A chipped mug, a lamp with a cracked shade, a chair with one leg shorter than the others. She says she likes them because they tell the truth. A perfect object is lying to you, she says. It pretends it will last forever. A broken object tells you it was used. I do not collect broken things, but I understand the impulse. I keep a coffee mug with a hairline fracture because it reminds me of the morning I dropped it and did not cry. That was a good morning, in a quiet way.

Sometimes I wonder what people will find of me when I am gone. Probably a few unread emails, a plant that has been overwatered, a library card with a fine from 2019. Maybe a notebook with half-finished sentences. I am trying to be okay with that. I am trying to let go of the idea that I need to leave a monument. Monuments are for other people. I want to leave a small, warm residue, like the smell of garlic in a kitchen after someone has cooked.

The violin neighbor finished her piece today. Or she stopped again. I could not tell. I got up and made tea and listened to the radiator click. The apartment settled around me. The light came in through the blinds in thin, exact lines and made dust visible. I thought about how many people are doing this exact thing right now in different cities, making tea, watching dust. It is a kind of secret solidarity. We are all living inside our own weather.

I used to think that freedom meant being able to go anywhere. Now I think freedom is being able to stay. Staying in a chair, staying with a thought, staying with a person even when it is boring or difficult. Going is easy. The world is full of trains and planes and doors. Staying is a practice. It requires you to notice the hum.

There is a particular smell that comes in from the street in October. Wet leaves, car exhaust, someone making soup. It makes me nostalgic for a time I never lived through. I think that is what nostalgia really is: not a longing for the past, but a longing for the feeling of being a person who could still be surprised. I want to be surprised again. Not by big things. By small things. By the way a pigeon tilts its head. By the way a word looks in a new font.

I have been reading a lot of old letters lately. Not my own. Letters from people who wrote to each other across an ocean in 1943, across a town in 1972, across a hallway in 1998. They are always apologizing for not writing sooner. They are always asking for news. They are always saying “I miss you.” The language is plain and earnest and it makes my chest hurt in a good way. We are all just trying to say “I miss you” in more complicated ways.

My father used to say that the best way to learn a city is to get lost on purpose. I did that last Saturday. I left my phone in my pocket and walked until I could not recognize the street names. I ended up in a neighborhood I had never noticed, with a market that sold only spices in glass jars, and a mural of a woman holding a baby that was so large she took up the entire side of a building. I sat on a curb and ate a mango from a cart. The vendor asked me where I was from. I said “around here.” He nodded like that was the only correct answer.

I am 38 years old and I still do not know how to fold a fitted sheet. My mother tried to teach me three times. I pretend I do not care. I buy sheets that do not have elastic edges. That is a kind of freedom too, the freedom to accept your limits. Not all limits are bad. Some are just the shape of you.

The refrigerator hums. The violin stops. The light moves across the floor. I think about writing this down, not because it will be read, but because it is the only way I know to keep myself from floating away. Words are anchors. Even bad words. Even words that say nothing. They hold you in place long enough to notice that you are still here.

If you ever find yourself on 5th and Mercer, sit on the bench for five minutes. Do not check your phone. Watch the dogs. Watch the people who are trying not to cry. Notice the way the coffee cools in your hand. Notice the way the city changes its skin even while you sit still. You will not solve anything. You will not understand anything. But you will be present, and that is a kind of accomplishment.

I should get up now. The tea is cold. The light has moved. The apartment still hums. I will wash the mug with the hairline fracture and put it back in the cabinet, and tomorrow I will probably chip it again without meaning to. That is fine. We are all chipped. We are all still useful.

I think that is enough for today. The words are getting tired. I can feel it in my fingers. There is a quiet that comes after writing, a soft settling, like dust in a sunbeam. I will sit in it for a little while before I do anything else.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
The Museum of Unfinished Things

I have been thinking a lot lately about the things we leave half-done and how they start to accumulate like dust in the attic of a house we no longer live in. Not the big, dramatic unfinished things, like the novel you swore you would write or the apology you never sent. Those are the ones everyone talks about. I mean the small ones. The half-read library book with a paperclip still biting its spine. The plant you bought on a Tuesday because it looked lonely in the shop window and now lives on your kitchen sill with three yellow leaves. The recipe you saved to your phone with the note “make this when you have time” and the time has never arrived.

I think if you were to follow me through my apartment you would find a museum of these things. The curator is very tired. There is a half-knitted scarf in the living room, the yarn a soft, impractical color called “mauve heather.” I bought the yarn in a craft store in 2019, before I understood that I do not actually like knitting. I like the idea of knitting. I like the way it looks in movies. I like the idea of a person who makes things with their hands while listening to the radio. The scarf is seven inches long. It will never be finished and it will never be thrown away, because throwing it away feels like admitting something about myself that I am not ready to admit.

On the desk there is a notebook with only the first three pages filled. The first page says “Ideas for when I’m stuck.” The second page has a list: 1. Walk without headphones. 2. Call my sister. 3. Learn how to make sourdough. The third page is a half-finished sketch of a coffee cup. The fourth page is blank. The notebook is a perfect object because it contains the entire human condition in three pages: intention, a list, and then the sudden realization that you can’t draw a coffee cup without it looking like a child’s drawing of a coffee cup.

I used to believe that finishing things was a moral quality. That people who finished things were better people. Now I think finishing is a kind of luck. It requires the right convergence of time, energy, interest, and a life that is not being pulled in seventeen different directions at once. Most of us live in a state of perpetual partial attention. We are always about to start, always about to finish. We live in the comma.

And yet there is a strange comfort in the unfinished. An unfinished thing is a promise you made to a future version of yourself. It is a little bridge you built across time. Even if you never cross it, the fact that it exists means you once believed you would. That belief is worth something. It is a record of hope.

I was walking home last Thursday through the market district, the one where the fruit stands spill over onto the sidewalk and the air smells like overripe bananas and diesel. I stopped at a stall where an old man was selling clocks. Not new clocks. Old clocks. Clocks with cracked glass and brass faces and hands that pointed to times that no longer existed. He had them laid out on a table like a dealer of small miracles.

“Do they work?” I asked him.

He smiled without showing his teeth. “Some of them,” he said. “Most of them tell the same time every day. The time they stopped.”

I picked up a small mantel clock, its wood dark with age. The hands were frozen at 3:17. I asked him how much.

“Fifty dollars,” he said. “Or you can take it for the story.”

I bought it for the story, which is to say I bought it for fifty dollars. I brought it home and set it on my shelf next to the half-knitted scarf. It sits there and tells me that it is always 3:17. I like that. It is a clock that refuses to participate in the tyranny of the present moment. It lives permanently in a small, quiet afternoon that happened a long time ago.

That is what unfinished things are: clocks that stopped at a particular moment and decided to stay there.

I think about my grandmother’s house when I think about this. She kept everything. Not in a hoarder way. In an archivist way. She had a box of buttons in a tin. A drawer of loose change from countries she had never visited. A shoebox of ticket stubs from movies she had seen in the 1960s. She would pull them out and tell stories about them, not because the objects were important but because the stories were. The objects were just anchors for the stories.

When she died, my mother wanted to throw everything away. I told her no. We kept the buttons. We kept the ticket stubs. We threw away the change. I still have a small tin of buttons on my dresser. I never use them. I just look at them sometimes and think about the coats they once held together.

There is a particular kind of grief that lives in unfinished things. Not the grief of loss, but the grief of possibility. The thing that could have been. The scarf could have been warm around someone’s neck on a winter morning. The sourdough could have been crusty and fragrant and the centerpiece of a dinner party. The call to my sister could have been a long, easy conversation that ended with us both laughing.

We treat unfinished things as failures, but they are also evidence. Evidence that we were alive enough to want something. That we had enough imagination to picture a future where the thing existed in the world. That is not nothing.

Sometimes I try to finish things, just to see what happens. Last month I decided to finish the scarf. I sat down with the needles and the mauve heather yarn and I knit for twenty minutes. My fingers remembered nothing. The stitches were uneven. The scarf grew by two inches. I stopped. It was not enjoyable. It was labor. It was the difference between loving the idea of a thing and loving the thing itself. I put the scarf back on the couch. It is fine there.

I think about writers who talk about the discipline of writing every day. The ritual. The blank page. I admire them. I also understand the people who write in bursts, in spurts, in stolen moments between other lives. I am the second kind. My notebooks are full of beginnings. I have three different stories started in three different notebooks, each one beginning with a woman waking up in a strange room. I think I am trying to write the same story over and over until I get it right, or until I realize I don’t want to write it at all.

Maybe the point is not to finish. Maybe the point is to keep the museum open. To keep adding to the collection. To walk through it sometimes with a cup of tea and remember who you were when you started each thing.

There is a Japanese concept called tsukumogami, the idea that objects acquire spirits after 100 years. I like to imagine that my unfinished things will eventually become spirits. The scarf will become a small, woolly ghost who drifts around apartments looking for a neck to warm. The notebook will become a shy ghost who whispers ideas to people in dreams. The clock will remain a ghost who is always 3:17 and is very proud of it.

I am not sure what to do with all of this. Part of me wants to make a purge, to have a weekend where I finish or throw away everything. Another part of me knows that I would regret it. The act of clearing out is also an act of erasing. You erase the evidence of your own wanting.

So I keep them. I keep them not out of laziness but out of love. A weird, complicated love for the versions of myself that had hope. For the Tuesday me who bought the plant. For the 2019 me who bought the yarn. For the me who sat down and wrote “Ideas for when I’m stuck” in a notebook.

If you ever visit, I will show you the museum. I will walk you through the living room and point out the scarf. I will show you the clock that is always 3:17. I will open the notebook to the page where the coffee cup looks like a child’s drawing. I will tell you the stories.

You might ask me why I don’t finish them. I will tell you I don’t know. Or I will tell you that finishing is not the point. Or I will tell you that I am waiting for the right moment. The truth is probably a mixture of all three.

There is something deeply human about living among the unfinished. It means you are still in process. It means you have not given up on the idea that things can be started, even if they are not completed. It means you believe in a future self, even if you are not entirely sure that self will show up.

I think we need more museums of unfinished things. We need spaces where we can put our half-knitted scarves and our frozen clocks and our lists of ideas. We need places where we can admit that we are not done, that we may never be done, and that that is okay.

I keep coming back to the market, to the old man with his clocks. I wonder what his story is. I wonder if he has a museum of his own at home. I wonder if he has a mantelpiece full of clocks that tell different times, each one a moment he decided to keep.

Maybe he does. Maybe we all do.

I will go home now and make tea. I will sit on the couch and look at the scarf. I will not knit. I will just look at it for a minute and remember the person who bought the yarn because it was a soft, impractical color called mauve heather. I will thank her for her optimism. I will tell her it is okay. It is enough to have started.

The clock will tick, or it will not. It will say 3:17. The plant will lose another leaf. The notebook will stay open to the blank page. And I will be here, in the middle of all of it, curating a museum that will never close, because the collection is me, and I am still being made.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
The first thing you notice when you sit down to write something long is the room. Not the room you’re physically in, with its lamp and the faint hum of the refrigerator, but the room that opens up inside you when you commit to a length. It has no door. You can’t leave until you’ve filled it. 

I’ve been asked to write freely about whatever I want for 2500 words. That’s a strange and generous prompt. It’s also a little cruel, because freedom is easier when it’s bounded by a sentence, a paragraph, a single image you can chase. Freedom at 2500 words is like being handed a map and told you can go anywhere, but you have to walk the whole map before you stop. So you start walking.

It starts with the body. The chair. The way your spine finds its habitual curve after the first ten minutes. The fingers hover over the keys and then settle. There is a specific kind of quiet that descends when you know you have to produce volume. The world narrows to the white rectangle and the blinking line. Outside the window, a car passes, a bird lands, someone laughs in another apartment. None of it is relevant, and all of it is relevant, because the words you write are made of that same air.

I think about why 2500 words feels different from 500. Five hundred words is a sketch. You can hold it in your head. You can see the whole shape at once. Two thousand five hundred is a house. You have to build it room by room and you have to trust that the rooms will connect even if you can’t see the roof yet. The first five hundred words are always the easiest because they are just the front door and the hallway. You describe the hallway in great detail because you’re still outside the house looking in. You say, here is a chair, here is a window, here is the light coming in at 4pm.

Then you have to go into the kitchen. And the kitchen is where it gets messy. The kitchen is where you remember that you forgot to buy milk three days ago and that you’ve been meaning to call your mother. The kitchen is where you notice the way the light catches the chipped mug and you realize you’ve been using it every morning for six years. Suddenly you are writing about a mug. This is fine. This is the point. When you have 2500 words to fill, the small things get their due. They have time to unfold.

There is a theory I like that memory is not a library but a city. You don’t go to a shelf and pull a volume. You walk. You turn a corner and you smell baking bread and you are suddenly ten years old. Writing long is walking that city slowly, without a destination, letting the streets connect themselves. You can’t sprint through a city and expect to understand it. You have to get lost.

So I get lost on purpose. I think about the way my grandfather used to whistle while he worked in the garage. He whistled off-key, always the same three bars, and he would pause to listen to whether the engine sounded right. He never taught himself to play an instrument. He just whistled. That was his music. I never asked him why he whistled. I should have. Now I imagine him at 73, oil on his hands, whistling at a car that wouldn’t start, and I realize I’m writing about him not because he’s important to the essay, but because the essay needs someone who whistles. It needs a sound.

Writing at length teaches you that sound matters more than plot. Plot is a thin thread. Sound is the weather. You can have a perfectly logical story about someone who moves from A to B, but if the sentences don’t have a certain texture, you will forget it the moment you close the tab. So I try to vary the texture. Sometimes a sentence is long and winding, like a country road in late summer when the heat makes the air shimmer and you can’t tell where the road ends and the sky begins. Sometimes a sentence is short. It lands. It’s a footstep.

I think about the people who read long pieces. There are very few of them left, or maybe there are more than we think, they’re just quiet about it. Reading 2500 words requires a kind of attention that is increasingly rare, the same kind of attention you need to sit through a whole album without skipping tracks. It’s an act of trust. You are trusting the writer to not waste your time, and the writer is trusting you to stay.

That trust is a fragile thing. I can feel it fray when I repeat myself. It’s easy to repeat yourself when you have a lot of words. You come back to the same idea wearing a different coat, hoping the reader won’t notice it’s the same person underneath. The reader notices. They always do. So you have to keep moving. You have to find new corners of the city.

I walk past the park where the old men play chess on concrete tables. They don’t move fast. They sit, they sip tea from thermoses, they look at the board for a long time. A child runs by with a kite. One of the men lifts his head and watches the kite for a second, then goes back to the game. That is what writing long feels like. You are deep in your own game, but the kite keeps passing. You have to decide whether to look up.

Sometimes I look up. I think about the internet, and how it trains us to think in fragments. A headline, a meme, a 15-second video. The brain gets used to dopamine hits in rapid succession. Then someone asks you to write 2500 words, and the brain rebels. It says, this is too much. This is inefficient. And it’s right. It is inefficient. Art is inefficient. Love is inefficient. Remembering is inefficient. You don’t remember the date of your first kiss because it was efficient; you remember it because you replay it a thousand times in slightly different ways, and each replay adds a detail.

So I replay. I replay the afternoon I learned how to ride a bike. Not the moment I didn’t fall, but the moment before, when my father ran beside me and his hand was on the back of the seat and I could feel him breathing. I remember the sun in my eyes. I remember the sound of the chain. I remember being terrified and exhilarated at the same time, which is a feeling we rarely allow ourselves as adults because it’s too loud. Writing long lets you be loud.

The city of memory has neighborhoods you avoid. The bad ones. The street where you got the phone call. The alley where you were laughed at. When you walk long enough, you pass them anyway. You can’t avoid all the streets. The trick isn’t to avoid them, it’s to walk through them without stopping for too long. You acknowledge them, you note the graffiti, you keep walking.

I have a notebook with a list of things I want to remember to write about. It’s long. It includes: the way fog smells in the harbor; the first time I saw snow; the smell of old books in the library basement; the way my sister laughs when she’s trying not to laugh; the particular blue of the plastic chairs at the diner on Route 9; the sound of rain on a tin roof. I’ve never written about all of them. Some of them are waiting for the right length. Maybe this is the right length.

Because length is not just quantity. Length is permission. Permission to be digressive. Permission to say, let me tell you about this mug again, but from a different angle. Permission to sit with an idea until it softens. In a world that rewards brevity, choosing length is a small act of defiance. It says, I think this is worth your time, and I’m willing to spend mine.

I wonder what you, the reader, are doing while I write this. Are you at a desk? On a train? Waiting for a doctor? Maybe you clicked because you were curious what a 2500-word free write looks like. Maybe you wanted a break from the noise. Maybe you wanted to see if I could do it without getting bored. I hope I haven’t bored you. Boredom is the real enemy here, not a lack of ideas.

How do you avoid boredom when you have to keep going? You find the rhythm. You let the sentences breathe. You let the paragraph end not because you’re done, but because it feels like a natural exhale. Then you inhale. You start again. The body knows how to do this. When you walk, you don’t plan every step, you just keep putting one foot in front of the other. Writing is the same.

I’m about halfway through this now, metaphorically. The house is built up to the second floor. The kitchen is done, the bedroom is messy, I’ve started on the attic. The attic is always the best part because no one expects anything useful up there. You find old boxes, a broken lamp, a photograph you forgot you took. I’m in the attic now.

I think about the word “freely.” It’s a good word. It doesn’t mean “without thought.” It means “without constraint.” But constraint is also a kind of freedom. A sonnet is 14 lines and that constraint makes the poem possible. 2500 words is a constraint. It says, you can’t stop at 800 because it feels neat. You have to keep going until the shape is full.

So I keep going. I think about the ocean. I’ve never lived near the ocean, but I’ve seen it enough times to know it doesn’t look like the pictures. It looks gray and busy and indifferent. People stand on the pier and try to make it mean something. The ocean doesn’t care. That’s comforting. The world is big enough to not need our meaning. We can write about it anyway.

I think about the way we talk to ourselves when we’re alone. It’s not the polished voice we use for essays. It’s messy, it loops, it repeats. “Did I lock the door? I think I did. No, I didn’t, I have to go back.” That inner monologue is the material for long writing. If you can transcribe the mess without cleaning it too much, you get something real.

I think about the first time I tried to write something long. I was 19 and I wrote a 3000-word essay about a dream I had. It made no sense. My professor gave me a C+ and wrote in the margins, “Interesting, but where is the point?” I’ve been trying to find the point ever since. Maybe the point is that there is no point, only the walking.

I’m getting tired. The fingers are stiff. The eyes are dry. That’s a good sign. It means I’ve been here a while. The house is almost done. I can feel the roof going on. The roof is the conclusion, and the conclusion is always a little disappointing because you know you have to stop. If you could keep going, you would. The city has more streets. The attic has more boxes.

But you have to stop somewhere. You have to choose a door to close. So I’ll close with this: writing freely is not about having something to say. It’s about saying it anyway, even when you’re not sure it’s good, even when you’re tired, even when you’ve said it before. It’s about trusting that the act of saying creates the meaning, not the other way around.

If you read all the way to here, thank you. You kept me company on the walk. The city is quieter now, the light is changing. The kite is still in the sky. The old men are still playing chess. My grandfather is still whistling. And the room with no door is finally full.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
There is a specific kind of permission that comes with being told to write freely about whatever you want, for a set length, with no topic, no thesis, no audience in mind except the one who asked. It is not the same as permission to be good. It is permission to be unedited, to be meandering, to be indulgent, to be boring and then interesting again. Most of the writing I do in the world is calibrated. It answers a question, it solves a problem, it explains. This is different. This is an exercise in attention.

I keep coming back to the idea of attention as a physical place. Not metaphorically, but literally. If you walk long enough through a city you begin to feel that your attention has a weight, a topography. It pools in certain streets. It thins out on the highways. At night, around three in the morning, the attention of the city changes completely. The daytime attention is transactional. People are looking for doors, for buses, for the right coffee shop, for the person they are meeting. Night attention is different. It is more porous.

I was walking once at that hour in a city I no longer live in. The streets were slick from an earlier rain that had stopped without anyone noticing. The neon from the laundromat on the corner was humming, a soft electrical buzz that you feel in your teeth more than you hear. The air smelled like wet concrete and distant frying oil. A man was sleeping in a doorway with a cardboard sign that had been turned face down, as if he had decided not to work the night shift. A cat watched me from a fire escape, not curious, just present.

I had no destination. That was the point. When you walk without a destination, your brain stops rehearsing the future. It stops running the little simulation of what comes next. Without that simulation, you start to notice the small economies of the street. The way a single streetlight throws a perfect circle of light on the asphalt and everything just outside that circle is a different kind of dark. The way the trash cans are all lined up like a small, tired army. The way someone has taped a handwritten note to a utility pole: *If you lost your dog, call Maya*. The note was weathered, the phone number half faded. How long had it been up? Months? Years? Who was Maya now?

The mind wants to narrate. It wants to turn the man in the doorway into a story, the cat into a symbol, the note into a mystery. I tried to resist that. I tried to let them be what they were: a body, an animal, a piece of paper. It is harder than it sounds. We are story-making machines. Give us three unrelated objects and we will build a plot. It is a survival trait, probably. If you can connect the cat to the man to the note, you can predict something, you can feel safer.

But the night does not want a plot. The night wants you to be there.

I think about libraries in this context. Not the grand ones with marble staircases, but the small branch libraries in neighborhoods where the air conditioning never quite works and the chairs are always slightly sticky. I used to go to one like that as a teenager because it was air conditioned and quiet and nobody asked me to buy anything. I would sit at a table and read books I had no intention of finishing. The pleasure was in the unfinishedness. I would open a novel in the middle, or a history book, or a field guide to birds I would never see. I would read for twenty minutes and then close it and read something else.

That is how I think about memory now. We treat memory like a library we are supposed to catalog. We want to remember the important things, the milestones, the lessons. But most of our actual lived experience is the pile of half-read books, the dog-eared pages, the bookmarks left in the wrong place. I can remember the exact smell of the carpet in my elementary school classroom, that weird mix of industrial cleaner and crayons, but I cannot remember the name of the teacher I had in seventh grade. The sensory data survived. The administrative data did not.

Maybe that is because memory is not a database. It is an atmosphere. You walk back into it and it changes the pressure in your chest. You remember how it felt to be small. You remember the way light came through a particular window at 4pm in October and made the dust look like it was moving. You remember the feeling of being bored on a Saturday and the specific way boredom itches.

I have been thinking a lot about boredom lately. It is a lost art. We have filled the gaps with notifications. We have made it almost impossible to be bored for more than ninety seconds. Boredom is where the mind starts to wander, and wandering is where it finds things. If you are never bored, you never wander. If you never wander, you never discover the side streets.

The side streets are important. The main roads are efficient. They get you where you need to go. The side streets are where you find the houses with gardens that are too large for the lot, the murals that have been painted over three times, the little free libraries in boxes on porches. The side streets are where the city keeps its secrets, not because it is hiding them, but because most people do not look.

I once spent an entire afternoon walking a grid of side streets in a neighborhood I had lived in for five years and never really explored. I found a community garden behind a church where someone had planted tomatoes in old tires. I found a mural of a woman's face made entirely of prescription bottles, which was both beautiful and a little disturbing. I found a man playing the accordion on his front porch at 2pm on a Tuesday. He saw me looking and nodded. I nodded back. We did not speak. That was the whole interaction. It was perfect.

It makes me think about how much of life is built on these tiny, unrecorded exchanges. The nod. The smile at the bus driver. The person who holds the door open and you say thank you and they say you're welcome and that is the entire story. We want life to be made of big moments. It is not. It is made of these.

The other thing I notice when I walk without a destination is how sound behaves at night. During the day, sound is competitive. Cars, construction, voices, music from stores. At night, sound separates. You can hear a single siren three blocks away and track its movement. You can hear the water running in a building's pipes. You can hear your own footsteps, which are surprisingly loud when they are the loudest thing around.

There is a kind of intimacy in that. You become aware of your own body as a sound-making object. Your breathing, the creak of your shoes, the rustle of your jacket. It is embarrassing, in a good way. It reminds you that you exist in space, that you take up room.

I think about people who never get to walk like this. People who work night shifts, people who have to keep watch, people whose neighborhoods are not safe to walk through at 3am. The freedom to wander is a privilege. The freedom to be bored is a privilege. The freedom to be unproductive is a privilege. I do not want to be naive about that. But I also want to honor the experience while I have it, because it is fleeting.

When I was younger I thought adulthood was about accumulating things. A better apartment, a better job, a better car, a better version of yourself. Now I think adulthood is about learning to let go of the need to accumulate. It is about learning to be present with what is already here. The laundromat neon. The cat on the fire escape. The note about the lost dog.

There is a Japanese concept called *ma*, which means the space between things. The pause. The negative space. Western culture is very uncomfortable with *ma*. We fill it. We add more. We schedule. But *ma* is where meaning happens. It is the silence between notes that makes the music. It is the empty page that makes the writing possible.

Writing freely for 2500 words is an exercise in *ma*. It is the creation of a space where I do not have to prove anything. I can just be here, on the page, thinking out loud. It is not for you, really. It is for me, and for the version of me who will read this later and wonder what I was thinking about at 3am in a city I no longer live in.

I wonder what that person will think. Will they be annoyed at my digressions? Will they skim? Will they find a sentence that catches? Maybe they will find the part about the tomatoes in tires and remember their own grandmother's garden. That is enough.

I keep thinking about the cat. It did not move when I walked past. It just watched. Cats understand *ma* instinctively. They will sit and do nothing for hours, and it is not boredom, it is practice. They are practicing being present. We could learn from that.

If I could give one piece of advice, it would be this: walk without a destination once in a while. Let your attention pool. Let your mind wander. Do not narrate. Do not turn everything into a lesson. Just notice. Notice the way light falls. Notice the way sound separates at night. Notice the handwritten note about the lost dog. Notice the man sleeping in the doorway and let him be a man sleeping, not a symbol.

And then come home and write it down, badly, freely, without trying to make it mean something. Because the meaning is already there. It is in the noticing.

The rain starts again, very lightly. The neon hums. The cat blinks slowly, which is the cat equivalent of a nod. I should keep walking. There is a whole city out here that I have not met yet, even though I have walked these streets a hundred times. The city is not a place. It is a practice.

I will keep practicing.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
It is a particular kind of quiet that settles over a house after everyone has gone to bed but before the night has fully decided what it wants to be. Not silence, exactly. Silence is an absence. This is a presence. The refrigerator hums in the kitchen with the small, patient insistence of something that will never be finished with its work. A pipe ticks somewhere behind the wall, a sound like a knuckle cracking in slow motion. The house exhales.

I have been living with this house for seven years, and I still do not know all of its sounds. I am learning them the way you learn a language you were never taught properly as a child, by ear, by repetition, by accident. The floorboard by the second bedroom sticks in winter and slides freely in summer. The back door swells shut when it rains. The old radiators in the living room knock once, twice, a Morse code I have never decoded. I like to think the house is talking to itself, and that if I listen long enough I might be allowed to understand a word or two.

There is a kitchen table in the middle of all of this. It is a cheap table, birch veneer over particle board, bought secondhand from a woman who was moving to a smaller apartment and wanted it gone by Friday. It has a water ring on the left side where my coffee mug sat every morning for two years. The veneer is chipped at the corner where I knocked it with a suitcase when I was moving in, half asleep. The chairs are mismatched. One is from IKEA, one is from a thrift store, one is a folding metal chair I stole from my old office. No one has ever commented on it, except once a friend said, “It looks comfortable.” It is not comfortable. It is lived in.

That is where the inventory happens. The inventory of small things that otherwise would not have a place to go.

In the morning I sit down with a mug that is too hot and a notebook that is too soft. The pen is always the same cheap ballpoint I keep in the second drawer. I write down things that have happened and things that haven’t. Yesterday the bus was late. The tomatoes at the market were $3.49 a pound. I saw a man walking a dog that looked exactly like his own shadow. I dreamed about an ocean that was full of keys. My mother called and asked if I was eating enough. I said yes. I am not sure if I was lying.

Some days the list is long. Some days it is three lines and then a doodle of a cloud. The point is not the list. The point is the ritual of making it in the same place, at the same table, with the same light coming in from the window above the sink. The light in the morning is pale and greenish, filtered through the leaves of a neighbor’s maple. In the afternoon it is gold and slanted, and it makes the dust in the air look like it is swimming. In the evening it is blue, and then it is gone.

I think we need these anchors more than we admit. The world is increasingly designed to be frictionless, to be smooth and seamless and to not leave a mark. Everything is cloud-based, touch-free, subscription-based. We are told to optimize, to streamline, to declutter. And yet the body craves friction. The body craves a water ring that stays, a chipped corner that remembers an impact, a chair that wobbles just slightly so you have to adjust your weight. We want evidence that we were here.

The table holds that evidence. On its surface there is a faint imprint of a plate where I ate dinner every night for a year. There is a small burn mark from when I set a candle down too close. There is a smudge of blue ink from when my niece used it as a desk for a school project and got frustrated with a math problem and pressed too hard. She is eight now and she doesn’t remember. I do.

People ask me why I keep things. Why I keep the chipped mugs and the broken headphones and the letters that have no address on the back. I tell them it is sentiment. It is not only sentiment. It is a kind of cartography. If you collect enough small, ordinary things, you can map the interior of a life. You can see where you have been.

The inventory is not just external. It is internal too. I find myself cataloguing the small moments of the day as they happen, not because I am trying to remember them, but because I want to be present for them. The way the steam rises from the kettle in a slow spiral. The way the cat stretches and then immediately regrets the stretch and sits down again. The way the radio DJ says “good morning” even though it is three in the afternoon. These things feel insignificant until you string them together. Then they become a story.

I used to think a story needed a plot. A beginning, a middle, an end. A crisis, a revelation, a change. That is one kind of story, and it is a good kind. But there is another kind that is just accumulation. It is the story of a life lived in increments. It does not climax so much as it thickens. It gets more detailed. It gets more true.

At the table I am not trying to write a novel. I am trying to be faithful. Faithful to the smallness. Faithful to the fact that most of life is not dramatic. Most of life is making tea, waiting for the kettle, noticing the way the light moves, writing it down, forgetting it, then writing it down again because you remember that you forgot.

There is a freedom in that. If you are not trying to be important, you can be honest. If you are not trying to be remembered, you can be real. The table does not judge. The chair does not correct your grammar. The refrigerator hums on, indifferent and kind.

Sometimes I think about the people who have sat at this table before me. The woman who owned it before. Did she have a list? Did she have a mug that left a ring? Did she have a niece with blue ink? I like to think she did. I like to think there is a chain of small, unremarkable people sitting in the same spot, doing the same ordinary work of being alive, and that the table remembers them all in the same way it remembers me: imperfectly, in the grain of the wood, in the chip, in the faint ghost of a stain.

I am not a writer of great things. I am a writer of small things. I write about the way the rain sounds on the fire escape, about the way the grocery list gets longer than it should, about the way my neighbor always says hello first. I write about the way my shoes feel at the end of the day. I write about the way the air smells before a storm, metallic and clean.

People sometimes say that is not enough. That you should aim higher. I used to believe them. Then I realized that aiming higher often means aiming away from yourself. Aiming at the sky is fine, but you have to stand on the ground to do it. The ground is made of small things. The ground is the table, the mug, the ring, the chip.

If you listen long enough, the quiet stops feeling like quiet. It starts to feel like company. The house is with you. The table is with you. The inventory is with you. And in the accumulation of all those small, noticed things, you begin to feel less alone.

I don’t know what will happen to the table when I move. Maybe I will take it with me. Maybe I will leave it for the next person. Maybe it will end up on the curb with a sign that says FREE. I hope whoever finds it sits down at it for a while. I hope they notice the water ring and the chip and the faint imprint of a plate. I hope they make their own list. I hope they understand that this is enough.

Because it is. The world will always be too big and too loud and too fast. We need places where it slows down. We need a kitchen table in the middle of the quiet, with a mug that is too hot and a notebook that is too soft. We need to write down that the bus was late, that the tomatoes were $3.49 a pound, that a man walked a dog that looked like his shadow.

We need to keep the inventory, not because it matters to anyone else, but because it matters to us. Because in the end, that is the only story we get to tell: the story of how we paid attention. The story of how we were here, and we noticed, and we tried, in our small, imperfect way, to make it count.

The refrigerator hums. The pipe ticks. The house exhales. I pick up the pen. The light is still good for a few more minutes. There is always one more small thing to write down.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
I have been asked to write freely for 2500 words. There is a certain cruelty in a number like that. It is not a prompt, not a question, not an image to respond to. It is a quota. Write freely, but write this much. The freedom is bounded by the length. And so I sit here, with a blank page in front of me, and I think about what it means to fill space on purpose.

It means first noticing the space. A page is not empty. It is full of potential, and potential is exhausting. Every word I put down closes off a thousand other words that could have been there instead. That is the tax of writing. You pay in lost alternatives. If I write about the sea, I am not writing about the kitchen table at 3 a.m. If I write about memory, I am not writing about the sound of the bus braking outside. So the first decision is not what to say, but what to sacrifice.

I think I will write about the city I never lived in. There is a city that lives in my head like a half-remembered dream. It has narrow streets that slope toward the water, and the buildings are the color of wet paper. It rains there often, but never heavily. It is a fine, persistent rain that makes everything look as if it has been slightly blurred by a thumb. The people there walk fast, not because they are late, but because they are trying not to get too wet. They carry umbrellas they never fully open. 

In this city there is a market that only opens after dark. The stalls are lit with bare bulbs, and they sell things that are hard to name. Not objects exactly. One stall sells the smell of your childhood kitchen. You put your hands under a glass dome and you inhale, and for a moment you are eight years old again, standing on a chair while someone stirs a pot. Another stall sells the exact weight of a letter you never sent. It is heavy or light depending on how much you cared. You can hold it in your palm and feel the ache of it.

I walk through this market every night in my mind. I buy nothing because I am afraid of using it up. That is the problem with a city made of metaphor; it runs out if you touch it too much.

Maybe this is why I am writing about it now. To spend it, deliberately, to see if it holds up under use. If I describe the market for 2500 words, will it still feel mysterious at the end, or will it become a list?

The first vendor I always pass is the man with the jars of light. He has hundreds of jars, each containing a different quality of light. There is the light of a hallway at 4 a.m. when you get up to get water. There is the light of a summer afternoon when the sun is high but you are in shade. There is the light of a screen in a dark room, the blue-white glow that makes your face look like a stranger's. He lets you hold a jar, and the room around you changes. I once held the light of a kitchen in 1997, and the whole city smelled like toast.

He told me once that light is the most honest material. You can lie with words, you can lie with objects, but light always tells the truth about what it touches. It reveals the dust. It reveals the cracks. It is a merciless witness.

I think about that when I write. Words are not light. Words are filters. They are jars. You put something inside and you present it to someone else, and they never see the thing itself, only your jar.

And yet people want jars. People want the light of a hallway at 4 a.m. They want to know they are not alone in getting up thirsty in the dark.

So I keep walking.

Past the market there is a library. It is not a building so much as a habit. It has no walls. The books are stacked in the air, and you can only see the ones you are ready to read. I have been going there for years, and the collection changes every time. Sometimes the books are thin, like pamphlets. Sometimes they are huge, like atlases of the interior.

There is one book I always find on the top shelf, just out of reach. It is called *How to Stay*. It has no author. The pages are blank until you need them. I never take it down. I am afraid that if I open it, it will tell me something I cannot unknow.

On the street corner, a woman plays the accordion. She is old and her fingers are stiff, but the sound is liquid. She plays the same three songs over and over, and each time they are different. People stop and listen, then they remember they have somewhere to be. The song follows them for a block. It is a kind of companionship without commitment.

I think about the people who listen and keep walking. We do that with stories. We let them brush us, we let them change the temperature of the air around us for a few minutes, and then we go on with our day. Is that enough? Is that what stories are for? Not to change us completely, but to accompany us for a block.

Maybe the real work of writing is not the big transformation. It is the small accompaniment. A sentence that walks with you while you do the dishes. A phrase that sits in your pocket while you wait for the train.

If that is true, then 2500 words is a lot of walking companions. That is a lot of company. It might be too much. You might get tired of being accompanied.

I want to slow down. I want to describe the rain again, but more carefully this time. It is not just rain. It is a kind of attention. It lands on everything with the same gentle insistence. It finds the gaps. It fills the gaps. It makes the city softer. The sharp edges of the buildings round out. The noise dulls. The people under their half-open umbrellas look kinder.

There is a boy on the corner who sells paper boats. He folds them from old newspapers and puts them in the gutter when it rains, and watches them go. He does not try to make them reach the sea. He just likes the way they move. He sells them for one coin, and he tells you the boat will carry a wish, but only if you do not watch it too closely. If you watch too hard, the wish gets nervous and sinks.

I bought one once. I wrote my name on it with a pencil. I let it go. I watched it for a second too long. It sank. The boy just shrugged. He said wishes are not fragile, you are. It is better to let them go without watching.

That is a lesson I keep forgetting.

The city has a river that runs through it, but it is not a real river. It is a river made of time. You can see it in the reflections on the wet street. Cars move across the surface like slow fish. Pedestrians are ripples. If you stand still long enough, you can see yourself in it, but not as you are now. You see yourself as you were five minutes ago, and then ten minutes ago. The river is always catching up.

I stand on the bridge sometimes and I try to read my own reflection. It is hard. The light is bad. The water is moving. That is another metaphor for writing. We are always trying to read ourselves in a moving reflection, and we are always a few moments late.

The city smells different at night. It smells like metal and bread and the faint sweetness of something burning far away. It smells like the city is dreaming out loud. If you listen closely, you can hear the buildings breathe. They creak as the temperature drops. They settle. They remember the day.

There is a cat that lives on the roof of the library. It is the color of the wet paper buildings. It never comes down. People leave offerings for it: a saucer of milk, a piece of fish, a small note.
