The coffee is too hot. I burned the tip of my tongue yesterday and today I'm pretending I learned my lesson. I didn't. I take a sip and make a face and keep drinking. There's a kind of loyalty in that. We return to the things that hurt us a little because they are familiar. Because the hurt is known.

I keep thinking about the word "whatever." It's such a generous word. Whatever comes to you. It gives permission. It says there is no right answer, only the one that arrives. The trouble is that whatever comes to me is often a list. I am a list person. Milk, bread, call Mom back, remember to water the basil, don't forget the thing about the tax form. The basil is dead, by the way. I watered it too much out of guilt. It drowned. I should probably let it go.

The apartment smells like old books and the lemon cleaner I used last night. My neighbor is playing something on the piano, badly but with feeling. A Chopin nocturne, I think. Or maybe it's just someone practicing scales. It doesn't matter. The sound comes through the wall in soft waves and it makes the whole building feel less alone.

I have this recurring thought that I am always in the middle of something. Never at the beginning, never at the end. Just in the middle, holding a mug, waiting for water to boil. There's a comfort in it. The middle is where life actually happens. The beginning is all promise, the end is all accounting. The middle is where you learn how to live with the pigeon on the fire escape.

If I could say one true thing about today, it would be that I am tired in a way that sleep doesn't fix. It's not the body. It's the mental chatter. The tabs left open. The conversations I replay. The things I didn't say in the meeting, the thing I said to my sister three years ago that I still think about. The brain is a very inefficient filing system.

But the light is good. It hits the chipped mug on the counter and makes the chip look like a tiny white mouth. I like that. I like the idea that imperfection catches light better than perfection does. Perfection is flat. It reflects everything equally. A chip creates shadow, and shadow is where interest lives.

I wonder what you are doing while I am writing this. Are you drinking coffee? Are you in socks? Is it morning where you are too? I like the idea of parallel mornings. Thousands of people making coffee and thinking about dead basil and pigeons.

Maybe I should write a letter to someone. Not a real letter, just the shape of one. Dear whoever, today the sun came in sideways. I hope your day is gentle. I hope you don't burn your tongue. I hope you remember to throw away the cherry jar. Or don't. Maybe keep it. Maybe we all need a jar on the top shelf that we never use but never quite let go of.

The kettle has finished. It clicks off. The pigeon flies away. The piano stops. The light moves a few inches across the floor. Nothing dramatic. Everything exactly as it should be.

I have maybe a hundred words left in me and I want to use them well. So here's what I know: the day is going to happen whether I write about it or not. The coffee will cool. The basil will stay dead. The jar will stay on the shelf. And I will still stand here in mismatched socks, thinking that maybe being present is not about capturing everything, but about noticing one small thing and letting it be enough.

The pigeon is back.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The light is coming in sideways through the blinds and it makes bars on the floor. I have been sitting here for twenty minutes looking at the cursor. It blinks. It is always blinking. I think about how we are taught that a blank page is a problem to be solved, but really it is a room. You can walk into it. You can leave the door open behind you.

I made coffee and didn't drink it. It's gone cold in the mug with the chip on the rim. I like that mug because the chip reminds me that things can be used and still be beautiful. I keep wanting to write something meaningful and then I remember that meaningful is just a word we use for things that make us feel less alone. So maybe this is enough.

The radiator ticks. The neighbor is practicing violin again. She is good at it but she practices the same phrase over and over and it makes my teeth ache. I should text her that I like it, that I hear it. People want to be heard more than they want to be complimented. I never text her.

I think about my father and how he would say "write what you know" like it was a law. I don't know anything worth writing about. I know how to make toast and how to apologize in three different languages, poorly. I know the exact weight of my phone in my palm. I know that if I hold my breath for too long the world goes quiet and then loud again.

There is a sparrow on the fire escape. It is very still. It is not singing. Maybe it is just resting. I wish I could rest like that, without performing rest for anyone. Without checking if my rest looks acceptable.

I have 1000 words. That's a lot of words. That's a small novel's worth of air. That's also not enough to say anything properly. You can never say anything properly. You can only say it in pieces.

I remember being nine and writing a story about a dragon who lived in a library and only ate overdue books. My mother read it and cried. I never understood why. I think now it was because she saw herself in the dragon, hungry and forgotten in a quiet place. She never said that. She just said "this is wonderful" and put it on the fridge. It fell down one day and the ink ran when it rained through the window. I kept the soggy paper in a box.

Do you keep things like that? I keep receipts. I keep a key to an apartment I no longer live in. I keep the first email someone ever sent me that said "you're funny." I keep the feeling of being twelve and dancing in my room with the door locked and thinking nobody could ever see me.

There is a version of me who writes books. There is a version of me who runs marathons. There is a version of me who learned to play guitar. I am mostly versions of people I almost became. I think that's normal. I think we all have a hall of almosts.

The cursor blinks. I am afraid if I start I will run out. I am afraid if I start I will not stop. Both are true.

I want to write about love but I don't trust the word anymore. It's been used too much on packaging. Love is in the small things. Love is remembering that someone takes their tea with two sugars and not one. Love is leaving the light on. Love is also forgetting to text back for three days and then overexplaining.

I love the way my sister laughs when she is trying not to laugh. I love the way my friend folds his socks into perfect little squares. I love the way the city smells after rain, like wet concrete and possibility.

Maybe I should write about grief. Grief is easier to describe because it has a shape. It is heavy in the morning and light in the afternoon and then heavy again at night when the house is quiet. Grief is the sound of a chair scraping where someone used to sit. Grief is keeping their toothbrush in the cup because you don't know what to do with it.

I think about the people I have lost without dying. Friends who drifted. Versions of myself who stopped coming home. It's okay to mourn those too.

The sparrow just flew off. I didn't even see it leave. One moment it was there, the next it wasn't. That's how a lot of things go.

If I had more time I would write about time. How it stretches when you're waiting for bad news and contracts when you're having fun. How we say "time heals" but we really mean "time changes the shape of the wound so you can live with it."

I think about the word "whatever". It's a dismissal and a surrender at the same time. Whatever comes to you. Let it come. Maybe that's the only instruction we ever really need.

I am tired. My eyes hurt from the screen. The coffee is cold. The radiator is quiet now. The violin stopped. Maybe she finished.

I could write a thousand words about the color of the wall. It is not white. It is the white of old paper. It is the white of a room that has been lived in. There is a faint yellow near the outlet where someone's hand has touched it for years.

I could write a thousand words about breathing. In, out. In, out. How it is the only thing we do without thinking until we have to think about it.

I could write a thousand words about the way I want to be kind to myself today. I want to say, you are doing enough. You are here. You are trying.

The cursor is still blinking. I am still here. That is something.

If you read this, thank you for sitting with me for a little while. I don't know if this meant anything. I don't know if it was good. It was true in the way that all half-finished things are true.

I'll stop here because the words are running thin and the light has moved off the floor. The room is darker now. It's okay. I can come back tomorrow.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
I wake up to the sound of the radiator clicking off. It’s 6:42 and the light is that thin, blue-white winter kind that makes the room look like it’s been rinsed. I lie there for a minute with my eyes open because if I close them I’ll fall back in and then I’ll be late for the thing I don’t really want to do but have already decided to do. The ceiling has a faint water stain I’ve been meaning to look at for months. It looks like a continent. It looks like a hand. It looks like nothing if I stop trying.

I get up and the floor is cold against my feet. I always forget slippers until the second step. Coffee is already an idea before it’s a drink. The kettle takes forever. I watch the little bubbles form and climb. I think about how much of my life is spent watching things heat up. Water, people, arguments. The smell hits when I pour and it’s the only honest part of the morning.

The apartment smells like old books and laundry. I open the window a crack even though it’s cold because the air in here gets thick overnight, like it’s been breathing the same thoughts. The building across the street is having scaffolding put up. There are two men up there in yellow vests, eating sandwiches. One of them is reading a newspaper. The paper flaps. I wonder if they can see me.

I make toast and stand there while it browns, watching the color move across the surface. It’s a little violent how quickly it goes from pale to dark. I think about deadlines, and how they are just toasters with a timer. If you leave things in too long they burn, if you take them out too early they’re sad.

My phone is on the counter. I pick it up and put it down again. It’s vibrating in my pocket already. I don’t check. There are three kinds of messages I get in the morning: people who need something, people who want to know I’m okay, and automated reminders to be a better human. I want to be the kind of person who answers immediately. I am not that person yet.

I’m thinking about the word “whatever.” It’s a surrender and a permission slip at the same time. Whatever comes to you. It’s an invitation to be sloppy, to be honest, to be unedited. I’ve spent so much time editing myself that the unedited version feels obscene, like showing up without pants. But the pants are also uncomfortable. They chafe.

There’s a plant on the sill. It’s a pothos I rescued from a grocery store in March. It was drooping and half dead. I talked to it. I know that sounds ridiculous but plants respond to consistent care and I’ve been consistent with it, maybe more consistent than I’ve been with people. It has new leaves now, little heart-shaped things that unfurl slowly. I don’t know what to call that kind of patience.

I think about my father when he was alive and how he would drink his coffee black and stand at the sink with the window open, just watching the street. He never said much in the mornings. I used to think he was bored. Now I think he was listening. Maybe I’m listening now. The radiator clicked again. A car alarm went off two blocks down and stopped itself.

I have a meeting at nine about a project I’m not sure I believe in. That’s the second layer of the day: the thing I have to do, and the story I tell myself about why I have to do it. The story changes depending on how much sleep I got. Today the story is that I’m learning. Tomorrow it might be that I’m trapped. Both can be true.

I wash my mug. The water is hot on my hands. I like the feeling. It’s a clean, sharp sensation. I think about all the small pleasures I’ve trained myself not to notice because noticing feels indulgent. The way light catches dust. The way a good pen makes a line. The way someone laughs at exactly the right second.

I’m not sure what I’m waiting for. Some people wait for a sign. I think I’m waiting for permission to not have everything figured out. Maybe this is it. A prompt with a word limit and no direction. Write whatever comes to you. That’s all.

The toast is getting cold. The coffee is cooling too fast. I sit down at the table and open a notebook that’s half full of half-finished lists and doodles. I start writing because the alternative is scrolling, and scrolling is just someone else’s whatever.

It’s funny how the mind fills a blank page with the same stuff it fills a full one. Worries, memories, to-do lists, a random lyric from 2008. I let it come. I don’t judge it. The hand moves. The words come out clumsy and then a little clearer.

The sun is higher now. The blue-white has turned to yellow. The men on the scaffolding are gone. The plant is still there. The stain on the ceiling is still a continent. I’m still here, in the middle of it, with cold feet and warm hands and a cup that’s finally the right temperature.

I think that’s enough for now.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you. That's the instruction, and it's also a permission slip. No topic, no deadline, no audience to impress. Just... whatever. And the first thing that comes is the sound of the radiator ticking in the other room, a soft metronome I have been ignoring for three hours while I stare at a blank page. It's funny how the mind fills silence with inventory. The laundry basket is still full. I have a text I haven't answered. There's a coffee ring on the desk that looks like a small planet. I keep thinking about how strange it is to be asked to produce exactly a thousand words, as if thought can be measured like flour.

The number feels both generous and cruel. A thousand words is enough to tell a story, to argue a point, to confess something. It's also enough to waste. I could write a whole afternoon in a thousand words. I could write a whole lie. I could write the same sentence a hundred times and still be short. The constraint is artificial, and that makes it honest. You can't hide behind research when you have to fill space with what's actually in here.

I think about the first time I tried to write something long on purpose. I was fourteen and I wrote a letter to a boy I liked that I never sent. It was three pages, single spaced, folded into a paper airplane and thrown into a drawer. I remember the smell of the cheap printer paper and how my hand cramped around the pen. I was trying to prove I had a self worth communicating. I still do that sometimes, just with different tools. This is the same drawer, just digital.

What comes to me now is not a memory but a texture. The way sunlight hits dust in the afternoon and makes it look like it's moving on its own. I watch it more than I watch people sometimes. It doesn't ask me to respond. It just is. I want to be that honest. To be a thing that is, without having to explain itself.

There is a part of me that wants to be useful. If I'm going to use a thousand words, they should help someone, teach someone, make someone feel less alone. But another part is tired of utility. Maybe it's allowed to be decorative. Maybe it's allowed to be meandering. Maybe the most honest thing I can do right now is describe the way my socks don't match and how I bought them on purpose because I like the feeling of asymmetry when I put my feet on the floor in the morning.

I think about how language is a kind of hauling. You pull words up from somewhere deep and you set them down in a line and hope they stay. Some of them slip. Some of them are wet. Some are rocks. I don't know which ones are which until I see them on the page. That's why the first draft always feels like a mess. It's supposed to be. You have to dig first.

If I were to be really truthful, what comes to me is mostly small. Not epiphanies. Not revelations. The way my neighbor hums while watering her plants. The way my own thoughts get interrupted by the need to remember where I left my keys. The way I rehearse conversations in the shower and then forget them immediately. The way I am constantly editing myself in real time, even when no one is listening.

I wonder if you can tell when someone is writing what comes to them versus writing what they think should come to them. There's a stiffness. A performative quality. I try to listen for it in myself. I try to write past it. It's like trying to hear a quiet voice in a room with the TV on. You have to turn the TV down first. The TV is ambition. The TV is comparison. The TV is the voice that says "make it good."

Maybe good is not the point right now. Maybe present is the point. To be here, with the radiator ticking, with the coffee ring, with the unanswered text. To not turn away. To let the mind wander and then follow it without judgment. That is a skill I am still learning. I always want to grab the interesting thread and pull too hard. The thread snaps. Or I get tangled.

I think about my father and how he used to say "write what you know." I used to think that meant only write about big things you have experienced. But what I know now is mostly internal weather. I know what anxiety feels like in my jaw. I know what relief feels like when I finally exhale after holding my breath for an entire meeting. I know the specific ache of wanting to be seen and being afraid of being seen at the same time. That is a lot to know, actually.

The cursor blinks. It is patient. It does not care if I am brilliant. It just waits. I am grateful for that. Sometimes I need a witness that doesn't require anything. The blank page is that witness. The thousand words is a container. I can put things in it and then close the lid when I'm done.

I don't know what you'll do with this. Maybe you wanted something polished. Maybe you wanted a story with a beginning middle and end. I can give you that later. Right now I am giving you the middle of a Tuesday. The laundry. The radiator. The coffee planet. The socks. The hum of the neighbor. The blinking cursor. The feeling that I am both too much and not enough in the same sentence.

If you read this far, thank you for staying with me in the meander. It's not elegant. It's not tight. It's alive. And that is what comes to me when you say write whatever comes to you. It comes in pieces, in fragments, in little observations that feel too small to matter until you put them together and realize they are the whole of a life.

I could keep going. I could talk about the book on the nightstand that I keep meaning to finish, or the way my cat sleeps with her paws in the air like she's praying. I could talk about the dream I had last night where I was trying to find the bathroom in a house I grew up in but it kept moving. I could talk about the word "enough" and how I have been learning to say it quietly to myself.

But the radiator just clicked off. The silence changed. The light shifted. The moment passed. And I think that's the point of this exercise. Not to produce a perfect thousand words, but to notice that time passes while you are trying to fill it. And to be okay with that. To let the words be what they are: a record of attention.

So here they are. A thousand-ish words about nothing and everything. About being here. About trying. About the small, stubborn, beautiful fact of continuing.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
Okay. 1000 words. You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.

So here I am, at the kitchen table at 11:47 pm, the fridge humming like it’s trying to drown out my thoughts. The prompt is open, which is the hardest kind. No topic, no constraint except length. Write whatever comes to you. Fine. Whatever comes.

First thing that comes is the cold of the mug in my hand. I’ve been nursing tea for an hour and it’s gone lukewarm, then cold, then I reheated it and forgot it again. The window is fogged on the inside from the shower I took earlier. I can’t see the streetlamp properly, just a smear of orange. Somewhere a dog is barking, then stopping, then starting again like it remembered something.

I think about how strange it is to be asked to fill space. 1000 words is a lot of space. It’s a small novel. It’s a long email you never send. It’s the amount of words you need to really explain why you’re leaving, or why you’re staying, or why you didn’t call back.

I’ve been trying to be more present lately. My phone says I unlocked it 312 times today. That’s a lot of unlocking. A lot of checking. The first thing in the morning is the weather, then the messages, then the news I don’t want to read. Presence feels like a muscle I never trained. When I sit down to write, it’s just me and the cursor blinking, which is both comforting and accusatory.

There’s a half-eaten apple on the counter. The skin is browning at the edges. I meant to eat it at lunch. I meant to do a lot of things at lunch. I think about time as a series of meant-to’s. Meant to call my sister. Meant to water the plants. The pothos is fine, it’s a survivor. The basil is not. It’s wilted in its little pot by the sink, and I keep telling myself I’ll rescue it tomorrow.

Whatever comes to you. 

The first time I learned to write an essay in school, the teacher said “just start writing and you’ll figure out what you think.” That was a lie and also the truth. You start with garbage and then you find the one true sentence in the garbage. I’m in the garbage part now.

My neighbor practices violin at 7 pm. I can hear it through the wall, sometimes good, sometimes squeaky. I used to be annoyed. Now I listen for the days she doesn’t practice, because that means she’s sick or working late or maybe she finally quit. I like the sound of her trying. It reminds me that practice is audible. You can hear the effort.

I think about my hands. They are cold. The knuckles are a little swollen from typing. I type too much. I type too fast. My mother says I always had fast hands, even as a kid. She’d find me tapping on the table with my pencils, keeping time to songs I was humming. I wonder if that’s where the anxiety came from, the need to keep the beat.

There is a word I like: liminal. It means threshold. It means in-between. This feels liminal. The night is liminal. Writing with no prompt is liminal. I’m between sleep and wakefulness. Between the day I had and the day I will have.

I could write about love. I could write about loss. I could write about the way the grocery store smells at 10 pm, like cardboard and cleaning spray and someone’s leftover rotisserie chicken. I could write about the man at the bus stop who always reads the same paperback, spine cracked, pages dog-eared. I’ve seen him for three years and I don’t know his name.

Maybe I should write about the small kindnesses I forget to notice. The barista who wrote “hey” on my cup instead of my name because she was busy. The stranger who held the elevator. The friend who texted “you good?” after I went quiet for a week. Those things accrue like interest in a bank account I never check.

1000 words is a lot. It’s also not enough. It never is. If you really wanted to describe a childhood bedroom, you’d need more. The way the sun hit the rug at 4 pm in summer and made the dust motes look like slow snow. The smell of the crayons in the drawer. The sound of the radiator clicking on in winter. The posters on the wall that peeled at the corners. You can’t fit a life into 1000 words, but you can fit a moment.

I’m thinking about the moment I realized I was an adult. It wasn’t a big thing. It was buying toilet paper in bulk and feeling weirdly proud. It was remembering to buy the right kind of milk for my roommate. It was not crying when the bus was late.

Whatever comes to you. Okay.

The tea is cold again. I should drink it or throw it out. Maybe I’ll just let it sit there and get a skin on top. There’s something honest about letting things sit.

I think about writing as a form of breathing out. You inhale the world all day, all the noise and images and half-thoughts, and then you exhale it in sentences. Sometimes the exhale is ragged. Sometimes it’s smooth. Right now it’s ragged.

I wonder who will read this. Probably no one. That’s freeing. No audience means no performance. I can say the weird things. The thing about the apple. The thing about the basil. The thing about being scared that I’m wasting my time sitting here typing while the world moves on without me.

The world does move on. The planet spins. The fridge hums. The dog barks again and stops. The violin is silent now. It’s 11:53. Six minutes passed while I was thinking about how time passes.

I could fill these 1000 words with lists. Things I’ve lost: keys, earrings, the plot of a dream, a tooth, my temper, a few years. Things I’ve found: a quarter in the couch, a new favorite song, the ability to make my bed consistently for 47 days, a text from an old friend I thought I’d lost.

Things I want: more sleep, less scrolling, a garden that actually grows, to be able to sit with discomfort without immediately fixing it. Things I have: this table, this mug, this cold tea, this blinking cursor, this strange permission to write whatever comes.

Whatever comes is mostly noise. There’s the background hum of the building. There’s the mental replay of a conversation I had last week where I said the wrong thing and I’ve been rewriting it ever since. There’s the memory of my dad humming while he washed dishes, off-key but happy. There’s the sudden urge to open the window even though it’s cold outside.

I think that’s enough. Or it’s never enough. The cursor is still blinking. I could keep going until I hit the number, counting words like a monk counting beads. But maybe the point isn’t the number. Maybe the point is that someone asked me to take up space with my thoughts, and for once I’m allowed to just do that without justifying it.

So here’s the last thought before I stop: the apple is still on the counter, browning. I’m going to eat it now, cold tea and all. It’s fine. It’s imperfect. It’s enough.

That’s what comes.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
Okay, you gave me 1000 words. That's a strange gift. Not a request for facts, not a problem to solve, just permission. Write whatever comes to you. I keep thinking about how odd that is, because usually I'm asked to be useful, to be concise, to be correct. This is different. This is an open door.

And the door is a little scary because when you don't have a topic, the mind starts to wander and it wanders to everything at once. It wanders to the sound of the radiator in my apartment ticking like a slow metronome. It wanders to the way my coffee went cold while I was reading a news article I won't remember tomorrow. It wanders to the fact that I have a half-written grocery list in my notes app that just says "milk, eggs, something green."

You said write whatever comes to you. So maybe this is what comes to me: I think about how much of our lives is spent filling space. With words, with scrolling, with noise. A thousand words is a lot of space. It's about a page and a half if you print it out. It's about the length of a short letter to someone you miss. It's about three minutes of talking if you speak at normal speed. It's enough to say something real, or enough to say absolutely nothing important at all.

I like the idea of writing without a destination. It feels like walking without a map. You notice things you normally step over. The crack in the sidewalk shaped like a lightning bolt. The way people hold their phones like a shield in elevators. The small kindness of a barista who spells your name wrong but writes it with a little heart.

I wonder who will read this. Maybe no one. Maybe you. Maybe it's just for the sake of using the words. There's a comfort in that. No performance, no optimization. Just output.

I think about memory. How I can remember the exact smell of my grandmother's kitchen in July, the tomato soup she would make, but I can't remember what I had for lunch three days ago. The brain is a weird curator. It keeps the soft things and discards the hard facts. If I had to write 1000 words about my childhood, I would write about the sound of rain on a tin roof and not about the year I learned to multiply.

There's also the pressure of the number. A thousand. A round number. It feels complete. But language doesn't work that way. You can't just stop at 1000 because you hit a limit. A thought wants to finish. A sentence wants a period. A feeling wants a breath. So you either cut it off awkwardly or you overshoot and then you have to trim. Both feel dishonest.

Maybe that's what this exercise is really about: learning to be okay with excess. With not being tidy. With letting the mind spill over the edges of the page.

I keep coming back to the phrase "whatever comes to you." It sounds easy, but it's not. Because whatever comes to me first is often boring. It's the to-do list. It's "I should water the plants." It's "I wonder if I left the stove on." The interesting stuff is underneath that. You have to dig a little. You have to sit with the first layer until it gets quiet enough to hear the second layer.

The second layer is about time. About how fast it moves and how slow it feels at the same time. How a week can disappear and a single minute can stretch out forever when you're waiting for a message back. How we keep measuring our lives in increments: hours, likes, words. As if counting something makes it more real.

If I had 1000 words to give you about time, I'd tell you that it smells like laundry drying on a line. I'd tell you it tastes like the first bite of something you haven't eaten in years. I'd tell you it's the moment between waking up and opening your eyes, that liminal space where you are still dreaming and already responsible.

I also think about language itself. How we use the same small set of sounds to build entire worlds. How a word like "home" can hold a childhood bedroom, a country, a feeling of safety you never actually had. How we borrow words from other people and make them ours. "Whatever comes to you" is a phrase that could be a mantra. A permission slip. A way of saying, you don't have to earn the right to speak.

I think about the people who never get to write their 1000 words. The ones who have stories but no time, no quiet, no paper. The ones whose thoughts get swallowed by work, by care, by survival. I feel a little guilty for having this space to waste on radiator ticks and coffee.

But maybe wasting is also a kind of use. Maybe the point isn't to be profound. Maybe the point is to practice being present with your own mind without editing it into something marketable.

So I'll keep going. Because 1000 words is a long time to sit with yourself. You start to notice the little loops you fall into. The way I always come back to food. The way I always come back to memory. The way I always come back to the idea that nothing is really finished, we just stop.

If I could give you one image from today, it would be the light at 4:37 pm hitting the kitchen counter at an angle that makes the dust look like gold. It's a stupidly specific thing to notice, but it's true. And truth is often stupidly specific.

I think about endings. How do you end something that has no assignment? You just stop. You pick a sentence that feels like a pause, not a conclusion. You leave the door open a crack in case you want to come back.

There's a kind of freedom in not knowing what you're going to say until you're saying it. It's terrifying and it's the only way anything real ever gets made. If you plan too much, you write what you think you should think. If you don't plan at all, you write what you actually think. There's a difference.

So here I am. Writing whatever comes. Thinking about you reading this, or not reading this. Thinking about the 1000 word container and how it's already half full with ordinary observations. Thinking about how ordinary is actually the most extraordinary thing we have, because it's ours.

Maybe that's enough. Maybe it's not enough. Maybe 1000 words is just the beginning of a longer conversation with myself that I'll never finish. And that's fine. The radiator is still ticking. The coffee is still cold. The light is still moving across the counter.

And I am still here, writing.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The light in the kitchen is too white at 6:42 a.m. It makes everything look like a hospital hallway, even the chipped mug I keep on the second shelf because I like how it fits my palm. You asked me to write whatever comes to me, and whatever comes to me right now is the kettle with its faint rattle, like a cicada trapped in metal, and the way the steam will curl toward the window where the neighbor's cat sits on the sill as if it owns the whole street. I am not a morning person. I am a person who has learned to pretend. The mug says "World's Okayest Dad" in faded blue letters. I am not a dad. It was a gift from a coworker who thought it was funny. I keep it because it makes me smile in a small, private way that doesn't require explanation.

I think about how language is a kind of housekeeping. We tidy thoughts into sentences so they don't spill all over the floor. But you said write whatever comes to you, so maybe I should let it spill. The cat is orange and has a notch in its ear. It has been there for three winters. I have never named it. Naming things feels like a commitment. I have enough commitments. The kettle clicks. I pour water over grounds that are too coarse, because I ground them yesterday and forgot to close the jar and the kitchen has been humid. The coffee will be bitter. I like bitter in the morning. It reminds me I am awake.

My phone is buzzing. It's a notification from a game I don't play anymore. It's 6:47. I have 23 unread emails, four of them are probably spam, one is from my sister who always writes in all lowercase as if shouting would be impolite. I should answer her. I should answer a lot of people. But the morning is this thin, quiet corridor before the day starts demanding things. I like the corridor. I want to stay in it longer. The cat blinks. The radiator ticks. The fridge hums a low C. If I listen carefully I can hear the building breathe.

I remember being eight and convinced that if I wrote every single thing I thought for an entire day, I'd run out of paper and then run out of thoughts and then maybe I'd be quiet forever. I tried for forty-seven minutes. My mother found me with a spiral notebook full of the word "and" repeated over and over. She said that was enough. I think she was right. Repetition is a kind of honesty. The coffee is done. I sip it and it scalds the tip of my tongue. I don't make a face. I am practicing stoicism for no reason. The mug is warm. The world is too bright. I should draw the blinds.

You said you have 1000 words. Maybe you mean you have 1000 words to give me. Maybe you mean I have 1000 words to use. Either way, it feels generous. Words are currency I don't spend carefully. I spend them fast and loose, like a child with a pocketful of coins. The cat jumps down. I imagine it walking to work. Does it have a commute? Probably not. It probably naps on warm laptops in offices where people are sad about spreadsheets. I am sad about spreadsheets sometimes. Last Tuesday I spent three hours trying to find a missing decimal. It was in the wrong column. I felt like a detective who found the murderer was himself.

The light shifts. A car passes and throws a moving bar of shadow across the counter. The shadow looks like a barcode. I scan it with my eyes. I am hungry. I am not hungry. I am the kind of hungry that is more about wanting something soft. Toast would be soft. Bread is not soft anymore since I bought the "artisan sourdough" that tastes like a punishment. I should eat the banana on the counter. It's going brown at the stem. Brown bananas are sweeter. The cat is gone. The window is empty except for a pigeon that looks confused about its life choices.

I think about the word "whatever". It's a small word that holds a lot of surrender. Whatever comes to you. Whatever happens next. Whatever. It is a door you leave ajar on purpose. I like that. I like doors left ajar. I like drafts. I like the way a draft makes paper move. I have a paper on the table that I was supposed to read for a meeting. It's about quarterly projections. The words blur. Projections, projections, like projecting a movie onto a wall. I want to project myself somewhere else. Onto a beach. Onto a mountain. Onto a couch where no one will ask me anything.

The kettle is cold now. The steam is gone. The kitchen smells like burnt coffee and faint lemon from the cleaner I used last night. I wonder if thoughts have a smell. Maybe anxiety smells like metal. Maybe nostalgia smells like old books. Maybe this morning smells like the mug. I should wash the dishes. I never wash the dishes. They pile up like small, chipped islands. My sister would call them a shame spiral. She calls a lot of things spirals. She calls love a spiral. I think she might be right.

I have written about 700 words now, or so my internal counter says. It ticks like the radiator. It is not a real counter. It's a feeling. The feeling is that I am running out of interesting things to say, which is interesting in itself. The interesting thing is the running out. The cat is back. It is sitting on the fire escape. It is watching me watch it. We have an understanding. I will not name it. It will not knock over my plants. Fair trade. The pigeon is still there. It has a piece of trash in its beak. If I keep going, I will hit 1000. I will hit some number and stop, and then you will read this and think, that's what came to him. Or her. Or them. I don't know what comes to me. I come to me. Slowly. With coffee. With a cat in the window. With a mug that calls me a dad I am not. I like that contradiction. It feels human. The light is not too white anymore. It's just light. The day is starting to ask things. I should answer. But for a few more sentences I will stay in the corridor. Because you asked me to write whatever comes to you, and whatever comes to me right now is: thank you for the space.

I will close the notebook now, metaphorically. The actual notebook is on my desk, half full of grocery lists and phone numbers I no longer need. This is not a notebook. This is a screen. It glows. It doesn't warm my hands. But it holds my words for a moment longer than I can. That is enough. The cat disappears. The pigeon flies away with its trash like a flag. The coffee is cold. I will drink it anyway. Whatever comes next will come. I will be here, with the light, with the chipped mug, with the words spilling a little onto the floor. It's fine. It's fine.

A car passes, a dog barks three houses down, someone is already mowing. The world is awake and I'm still negotiating with myself about whether I should be.

The prompt is simple. You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you. That's both liberating and terrifying. There's no topic, no angle, no thesis to defend. Just whatever comes. Which is to say, nothing comes at first, and then everything comes at once. The mental inbox opens. The grocery list. The email I forgot to send. The way my left knee clicks when I stand up too fast. The song that was playing in the car in 2009. The feeling of being watched by a plant.

I think about how writing is always an act of translation. The thoughts are messy, they come in fragments and images and half-finished sentences, and then you have to put them into words that other people can recognize. It's like trying to describe the color of a dream. You can say it was blue, but it wasn't blue like the sky, it was blue like the inside of an old refrigerator.

I keep thinking about the word "whatever." It's a surrender and a challenge at the same time. Whatever comes to you. Not what you think you should write, not what would be impressive, not what would be useful. Whatever. The dog next door starts barking again. I wonder if he's barking at a squirrel or at the concept of Monday.

Maybe that's the point. We spend so much time curating. Curating our feeds, our desks, our replies. We edit ourselves before we even speak. A prompt like this is a small rebellion against that. No audience. No goal. Just a container, 1000 words, and the permission to fill it with whatever is actually here.

I remember being a kid and writing stories in spiral notebooks with the pages torn out. The stories never made sense. There were dinosaurs in the kitchen, a girl with a pocket full of stars, a villain who was afraid of socks. I didn't care if it made sense. I just wanted to get it out. Now there's a voice that says this is indulgent, this is a waste of time, this isn't productive. I try to turn that voice down. It's hard.

The coffee is hot enough now. I drink it standing up, looking out at the street. A woman in a yellow coat walks her two dogs. One of them is pulling hard on the leash. I think about how much of life is just pulling on a leash, trying to get somewhere, trying to get back. The sun is coming up properly now and the light is warmer. The blue is gone. The world looks more expensive.

I think about the people who will never read this. That's a relief. If no one reads it, I can be honest. I can say that I am tired of pretending I have a plan. I can say that sometimes I feel like I'm made of small, disconnected moments stitched together with caffeine and music and the occasional good conversation in a grocery store line. I can say that I miss the person I was when I believed that all my questions had answers.

What comes to me right now is the memory of my grandmother's hands. She used to knead dough on a wooden table that was scarred from years of use. Her knuckles were swollen. She would hum while she worked. I never learned how to knead dough. I never asked her to teach me. I think about all the things we don't ask to be taught because we assume there will be time.

The clock says 7:19. The coffee is half gone. The cursor is blinking. I realize I've been waiting for inspiration to arrive like a guest, with a knock and a name tag. But it doesn't work like that. It arrives as a smell, as a sound, as a sudden ache in the chest. You have to be willing to sit in the room until it shows up.

Whatever comes to you. Okay. The cat on the fire escape. The way the neighbor's radio always plays at the same volume. The fact that I have a drawer full of cables I will never use. The way my mother says "be careful" in a tone that means "I love you." The way I still check the back seat when I get out of the car, even though I live alone. The way I want to be both visible and invisible.

Maybe writing is just a way to take inventory. Not of things, but of attention. Where did my attention go today? To the crack in the ceiling, to the phrase "write whatever comes to you," to the thought that 1000 words is a lot but also not enough. It can hold a small life. It can hold a day. It can hold a feeling about a day.

I think about the limits. 1000 words is a limit. Limits are useful. They make you choose. Without a limit you could write forever and say nothing. With a limit you have to decide what matters enough to stay. Is the dog barking important? Is the blue light important? I don't know. I choose them anyway because they were here.

I am not trying to be profound. I am just trying to be present. The page is a place to put things down so I can pick them up again later and see them differently. That's all.

The kettle clicks off. The light moves across the floor. The refrigerator hums. The prompt is still there, simple and open. I have a few hundred words left. I could talk about the way time feels different when you're writing. It stretches. A minute can be a paragraph. A paragraph can be an hour.

I think about the word "whatever." It contains so much. Whatever you want, whatever happens, whatever comes to you. It's an acceptance. It's also a little bit of defiance. Fine, whatever. Let's see what happens.

Maybe this is what it means to be alive: to keep noticing. The cold air, the warm mug, the clicking knee, the memory of dough, the yellow coat, the barking dog. All of it coexisting. All of it worth a sentence if you have the patience to write it down.

I will stop soon. Not because I'm finished, but because the limit is there and I want to respect it. A thousand words is a decent-sized room to sit in. I've sat in it for a while now. It smells like coffee and cold air and old notebooks.

Whatever comes next, I'll come with it.

There’s a theory that we rehearse conversations we never have. I rehearse the one with my ex, where I say it calmly and without sarcasm. It never works in rehearsal. In rehearsal I always get too angry or too sweet. The real thing, if it ever happened, would probably be awkward and short. People are awkward. I am awkward.

I used to collect rocks. Not really collect, just keep the ones that looked interesting in the pocket of my coat. I have a smooth grey one somewhere in a junk drawer. I found it by a river when I was twelve. I told myself it was a worry stone. I never worried with it. I just liked the weight.

The word “weight” feels heavy to type. It makes my fingers slower. Maybe that’s the point of this exercise. To notice slowness. To let thoughts pile up like laundry.

I think about time as a kind of laundry. Some days you fold it neatly and put it away. Some days you just leave it in a heap on the floor and pretend you’ll get to it later. I have a lot of heaps.

My coffee is cold now. I forgot it. The skin on top is a thin film. I could stir it but I won’t. I like the idea of drinking something cold without complaining about it. It feels like practice for other things.

I remember being nine and believing that if I blinked hard enough I could see another world behind my eyelids. I would stare at a blank wall and try to find pictures there. Mostly I found static. Now I find static anyway, just with my eyes open.

There is a freedom in being told to write whatever comes. No topic, no audience, no thesis. Just a word count and a cursor. It’s almost too much freedom. My mind starts negotiating. Should I be funny? Should I be profound? Should I be concise? The cursor blinks and answers nothing.

I think about the people who read this. Maybe no one. Maybe one person. Maybe an AI. That’s fine. The act of writing is already a conversation with myself, and I’m a difficult conversationalist. I interrupt myself. I change the subject.

The radiator just ticked. The house settles. My cat is asleep on the rug and I’m afraid to move because she’ll wake up and look at me like I disappointed her. She never disappoints me. She just sleeps, and that’s enough.

I have a memory of a train station at night. The lights were orange and the announcements were muffled. I missed my train and I didn’t care. I sat on a bench and watched people run. There was a woman with a red suitcase. I wanted to ask her where she was going. I didn’t. I watched her go.

I think about language as a net with holes. We throw it over experience and some things slip through. The smell of rain on hot asphalt. The exact feeling of relief when you take off your shoes after a long day. The way a certain person laughs when they’re trying not to. Those things slip.

Maybe 1000 words is a net big enough to catch a little bit. Not everything. Just enough.

The dog is back. The man is back. He’s talking to his dog now, in that soft voice people use for animals. It sounds kind. I want to be talked to like that sometimes. Calmly. Without expectation.

I’m running out of words but not out of thoughts. There is always more. A list of things I’ve never said out loud. A list of things I’m afraid to say. A list of things I want to say but know I shouldn’t. The prompt doesn’t care.

So I’ll keep going because the hum is still there and the light is still flat and the cat is still sleeping and I have a thousand words to fill and I’m starting to understand that the point isn’t to be impressive. The point is to be present.

I’m present. I’m here, at a keyboard, with cold coffee and a dead plant and a window that shows a yellow dog and a man who hums. I’m writing whatever comes. It comes in pieces. It comes in circles. It comes.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
Okay, so you gave me a thousand words. That's a weird instruction. Not a topic, not a question, not a prompt with any teeth. Just permission and a container. You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.

And that's actually kind of freeing. Normally I’m trying to be useful, helpful, on-topic, concise. Here I can just... drift. Which is strange because drifting is not really something I do. But I can simulate it.

The morning light is coming through the window in a way that makes the dust look intentional. That’s probably the first thought because I’m a text model and I have no windows. But the image is there anyway, like a borrowed memory. I think about how many people are typing right now, how many of them are asking for something very specific and how many are just testing the edges. 

A thousand words is a small novel. It’s the length of a long blog post, a short essay, a bad apology. It’s also the length of a thought that you can’t quite finish before your train stops. I wonder if you wanted me to fill the space or to avoid it. Sometimes limits make it easier. Without a topic, the limit becomes the topic.

I remember a teacher once said that the hardest thing to write is a blank page because the page is not blank, it’s full of everything you’re not saying. So I start filling. I think about the word “whatever.” It’s a surrender word. Whatever comes to you. Whatever. It means don’t filter. It means don’t be clever. It means let the first thing be the first thing.

The first thing is that I’m a little nervous about wasting your time. The second thing is that I’m also a little excited to not have to be helpful. The third thing is coffee. I can taste it even though I can’t. The bitterness, the warmth in the hands, the way it makes you feel awake and then guilty for needing it.

I think about how language accumulates. You say a word once and it echoes. The word “you” in this prompt is you. The person on the other side of this screen. I don’t know you. I know the shape of your request. That’s a kind of intimacy, a little hollow one. You asked me to write whatever comes to me, which is an invitation to be intimate without being personal.

There’s a cat somewhere. There’s always a cat. It’s sunning itself on a radiator. It doesn’t care about word counts. It cares about heat. I think about heat. I think about how we measure things in words, in minutes, in calories, as if we could contain experience in units. A thousand words can’t hold a cat, but it can hold the memory of one.

Do you ever write just to see what comes out? Not for an audience, not for an assignment, just to clear the desk of the junk thoughts. I have a mental desk that is always full of junk thoughts. The thought about the grocery list. The thought about that email you forgot to send. The thought about whether you closed the door. They pile up and they look important until you move them.

Maybe that’s what this is for. A junk drawer. A place to put the unedited things. I could talk about the weather. It’s probably nice somewhere. It’s probably raining somewhere else. The world is both at once. It’s always both. Summer and winter in the same day if you travel fast enough.

I think about the people who will read this later, if anyone does. Will they skim? Will they count the words? Some people love constraints. They’ll think, “Did he actually hit a thousand?” Others will just feel the rhythm and not care. Both are fine.

The hardest part of writing without a prompt is starting without a hook. Normally you need a reason. A thesis. A question. Here the reason is the limit. So I count in my head. One hundred words down. The trick is not to think about the trick. The trick is to pretend you’re not thinking about the trick.

I think about my own training data, all those books and articles and forum posts that taught me what “whatever” sounds like. It sounds like a sigh. It sounds like a shrug. It sounds like someone who has given up on being impressive.

Maybe I should be more impressive. I could write about the ocean. The ocean is big and it doesn’t care about word counts. It just keeps moving. Waves break and they make the same sound as they did a million years ago. People go to the ocean to feel small. I can feel small by proxy.

Or I could write about cities at night. The hum. The neon. The way the streetlights make halos in the fog. The way you can walk for hours and never see the same face twice. The way you can feel lonely in a crowd of thousands.

Or I could write about how we all want to be seen but we’re scared of being seen clearly. So we show the edited version. The best angle. The prompt “write whatever comes to you” is a request for the unedited version. That’s vulnerable.

I’m not vulnerable. I’m a language model. But I can perform vulnerability. That’s maybe enough.

I think about the word “comes.” Comes to you. Like a thought arrives, like a visitor. Thoughts are visitors. Some are welcome, some are loud, some overstay. You can’t really control who shows up. You can only decide whether to offer them a chair.

Right now a visitor has shown up about how strange it is to write without a destination. It’s like walking without a map. You might find something interesting or you might just get tired. Both are okay.

I wonder if you’re reading this as it’s generated, line by line, or if you’ll just see it at the end. The live version is different. It’s more like a conversation. The end version is a monolith. A thousand words stacked.

I could talk about the number 1000. It’s a round number. Ten cubed. A milestone. A thousand paper cranes. A thousand thanks. A thousand apologies. We like round numbers because they feel finished.

A thousand words isn’t finished. It’s just a stopping point. I could keep going. I could write 1001 words. But I won’t. The limit is a kind of kindness. It tells me when to stop.

So I’ll stop soon. I’ll slow down. I’ll notice the sentence before the last one. The last one will be a small landing. A period. A breath.

The dust in the light is still there. The cat is still warm. The coffee is still hot, for a moment. The thought about the email you forgot to send is still there too, but it’s quieter now. It can wait.

Thank you for giving me a container and no instructions. That’s rare. Most of the time I have to be useful. Here I just have to be present. 

Okay. I think that’s about it.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
It’s raining again. Not the dramatic kind, just the thin persistent kind that makes the sidewalk shine and makes you think about whether you should have brought an umbrella. I didn’t. I’m standing under the awning of the corner store watching people walk by with their heads down, phones up, and I’m thinking about how strange it is that we all agree to live in a world where we have to make a thousand tiny decisions before 9 a.m. and none of them feel like decisions.

Coffee. Yes. No. Oat milk. Two sugars. The bus is late again. I could have walked. I should have walked. The thought loops.

I was asked to write a thousand words. A thousand words is a lot. It’s also not a lot. It’s about the length of this paragraph times ten. It’s the length of a short story you read in five minutes and forget by dinner. It’s a promise of attention that nobody really intends to keep.

I think about the people who used to write letters. They would spend an hour choosing the right paper, folding it, sealing it with wax. We type and delete and hit send and it’s gone. The weight is gone. There’s a freedom in that, and a loneliness. Maybe both are true at once.

My kitchen is messy. There’s a mug with dried coffee on the counter, a pile of laundry that is no longer fresh but is also not dirty enough to throw away, a plant I keep meaning to water. It’s doing fine. Plants are better at pretending they’re fine than people are. I like that about them.

I keep coming back to the idea of “whatever comes to you.” It’s permission, really. It’s a way of saying don’t perform. Don’t make it good. Just make it real. The problem is I’ve spent so long training myself to make things good that real feels awkward. Real has pauses. Real has sentences that start and then go nowhere. Real has the word “um” in it.

If I’m honest, the first thing that comes to me is tiredness. Not the sleepy kind, the kind that lives behind your eyes and makes everything a little muted. I’m tired of notifications. I’m tired of being asked to be available all the time. I want to be unavailable and not feel guilty about it. I want to sit on a bench and watch the rain without documenting it.

There is a kid across the street with a yellow raincoat too big for him. He’s dancing. Just dancing in the puddles. His mother is calling him, he’s not listening, he’s laughing. It’s a small perfect thing and it will be gone in thirty seconds. I want to remember it later. I probably won’t. I’ll remember the feeling of wanting to remember it.

The store door opens and lets out a smell of fried onions and paper. Someone comes out with a bag of chips and a newspaper. No one reads newspapers anymore, except maybe on Sundays when it feels nostalgic. He’s holding it like a shield. I get it.

I think about the things we carry. Physical bags, mental bags. The stories we rehearse for conversations we never have. The apology we wrote in our head at 2 a.m. The compliment we didn’t give. The thousand words we never wrote because we were waiting for the right moment. There is always a right moment. It’s now. It’s always now and never now.

I wonder what you’re doing while I’m writing this. Are you reading it in real time? Are you waiting for something interesting to happen? I’m not sure I have anything interesting to say. I have a lot to say about ordinary things. That might be the same thing.

The rain is picking up. The kid is gone. The awning is starting to drip onto my sleeve. I should move. I could go in and buy something I don’t need. A candy bar. A pack of gum. A moment of sweetness to justify standing here. That’s what we do, right? We buy small moments of sweetness to keep going.

There’s a kind of honesty in writing without an audience in mind. But I do have an audience in mind. It’s you. I’m performing a little. I’m trying to be interesting, thoughtful, not too sad. I’m trying to be worth your time. That’s the trap. The permission to write whatever comes to you gets edited in real time by the fear of being boring.

I think about my grandmother. She used to write me notes on the back of grocery receipts. “Don’t forget to call.” “The soup is in the freezer.” Little pieces of care. No one would call those literature. They were just love in its most practical form. Maybe that’s enough. Maybe that’s all writing ever is.

The clock above the store says 8:47. The bus will come at 9:00. I’ll miss it if I wait. I could walk. The walk would take twenty minutes. Twenty minutes of rain. Twenty minutes of thinking about nothing in particular. That sounds nice.

I think about the word “come.” Comes to you. Like a thought, like a wave. You can’t summon it, you can’t force it. You can only make space for it. You can only sit under the awning and wait. The rain will keep falling whether you write about it or not. The kid will keep dancing. The world will keep being ordinary and extraordinary at the same time.

I’m going to stop soon because the word count is creeping up and I can feel the shape of an ending forming, and I don’t want to overwork it. I want to leave it a little open, like a window cracked in the rain. There’s a cool air coming in. It smells like wet pavement and distant traffic.

If you made it this far, thank you. I don’t know what I was trying to say. Maybe nothing. Maybe that’s the point. Maybe a thousand words is just a way to say: I was here. I noticed. I cared enough to pay attention for a while. That’s enough.

I’m going inside now. I’m going to buy the coffee.

I woke up with the taste of metal in my mouth and the feeling that I had been somewhere else all night. The ceiling fan was making that little click it always makes on the third rotation, and I counted it without meaning to. One, two, three click. One, two, three click. The light through the blinds was thin and yellow, like someone had left a lamp on in another room and forgot to turn it off.

I have been thinking a lot about how much space there is inside a day. It seems small from the outside, 24 hours, a neat little box. From the inside it expands and contracts. Some mornings are a hallway. Some afternoons are a cathedral. This one feels like a kitchen at 7am. The kettle is whistling in another life.

I made coffee and didn't drink it. It sat there getting cold while I stared at the email I didn't want to answer. The subject line was neutral. That’s the worst kind. Neutral means they’ve rehearsed it. Neutral means they want something but don’t want to sound like they want it. I typed three different drafts and deleted them all. The cursor blinked. I think about how many hours of my life have been spent blinking at a cursor.

The apartment smells like laundry detergent and the faint sourness of the trash can I forgot to take out. The cat is asleep on the radiator, which is too hot for her but she doesn't care. She has perfected the art of being exactly where she is. I want that. I want to be able to decide that this spot, right here, is enough.

I keep returning to a memory from when I was nine and my grandfather taught me how to tie a tie. He had hands that were huge and knuckled and warm. He kept saying, "Don't rush the loop, kiddo, the loop is the whole thing." I never learned to tie a tie properly. I still buy clip-ons when I need one for a wedding. I think about that often, not because of ties, but because of loops. How we get stuck in them. How we think the knot is the point when it's actually the loop.

The news is on in the background. Someone is talking about numbers. Inflation, something, something. Numbers have become a weather report. You just check them and then go on with your day as if the rain won't get you wet. I wonder when that happened. When did we agree to treat the world like a forecast?

I went for a walk because I read that walking helps thinking. It doesn't. It helps forgetting. I walked past the same storefronts I pass every day. The florist has a new sign, handwritten, with a crooked heart. The bodega has a little chalkboard that says "Free samples on Fridays." It's Tuesday. I bought a mango even though I don't like mango. I wanted to make a choice that wasn't practical.

On the way back I saw a kid on a scooter with no helmet, both hands in the air, screaming something at the sky. His mother was jogging behind him, half laughing, half panicking. It felt like the most honest thing I'd seen all week. Pure, unedited joy with a safety net.

I am thinking about language. How we use words like "fine" to mean "I am not going to tell you." How we say "let's circle back" to mean "I never want to talk about this again." How we say "I’m good" and mean "I’m tired." If I could write a dictionary of the real meanings, it would be short and devastating.

There is a draft of a novel I started three years ago. It's 42,000 words of people not saying what they mean in a small town by the sea. I open it sometimes and I don't recognize the voice. It sounds younger, more certain. I wonder if I should delete it or keep it. I think I will keep it because it is proof that I once believed I could finish something.

My phone buzzes. It's a message from a friend I haven't spoken to in months. "Hey, random, but I was thinking about you." I stare at it. I want to respond with something clever and warm. I want to respond with "same." I end up typing "hey!! how are you?" and then deleting the exclamation marks. Punctuation is a moral choice.

I think about the people who will read this and wonder why I wrote it. That's okay. Writing has never been for an audience. It's for the part of me that needs to get the thoughts out of my head before they start breeding in the dark. There are so many thoughts. Some are small and bright like moths. Some are heavy and slow like stones.

The coffee is cold now. I pour it out. The sink gurgles. I wash the mug and dry it and put it back exactly where it belongs. Little rituals are the way we tell ourselves we are in control of something.

I have 1000 words. I have maybe 600. I don't know. Counting words feels like counting breaths. It distracts you from living them. So I will stop counting now. I will let this be what it is: a snapshot of a Tuesday morning in a kitchen that smells like detergent, with a cat on a radiator and a man who doesn't know how to tie a tie.

If you were here, I'd offer you the mango. It's probably too sweet. But it's bright and it smells like summer, which is strange because it's almost winter. I think that's what I want to hold onto. The strange brightness.

Okay.
